speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF ISRAEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the house I should like to refer to the presence in the gallery of the Prime Minister of Israel, Mr. David Ben-Gurion, the valiant nation builder of modern Israel. He is not unknown to Canada, having been here on more than one occasion, the first of which was in 1917 or 1918 when, following the Balfour declaration for the acceptance of the setting up of a national home for the Jews, he belonged to the Royal Fusiliers who were then taking their training in Windsor, Nova Scotia.
Throughout the years he has given leadership to his country. Our distinguished visitor is no stranger to parliament. He has served in the knesset, the parliament of his country, for many years, and represents that belief in parliamentary democracy which has been an essential element of his life and dedication. He comes from a land where our religious faith originated and from which many of the values of western civilization have been derived. Since the creation of his country in 1948 the people have been engaged in a remorseless struggle against climate and economics. As the leader of that nation he has earned admiration for the perseverance which has enabled him and those associated with him to meet almost insuperable obstacles in the directions I have indicated.
We welcome him to Canada for the position which he occupies, and for the contribution that the people of the Jewish race have made to Canada over a period of slightly more than 200 years. I am sure I speak for hon. members everywhere when I say that we extend to him the warmest of greetings and good wishes, and through him to the president and people of Israel.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF ISRAEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Leader of the Opposition and on behalf of the Liberal opposition I am happy to join the Prime Minister in extending a sincere welcome to Canada and to this
parliament, to the distinguished Prime Minister of Israel, the head of government in that dynamic little state.
On the occasion of his visit to this parliament it is appropriate that we should remind ourselves that Canada has been in the forefront of almost every vital step in the development of the state of Israel since 1947, when partition was first voted. This, too, is an occasion to recall that partition itself was urged and actively supported by the Canadian representative on the United Nations special committee on Palestine, Hon. Mr. Justice Rand, then of the Supreme Court of Canada. It was he who, along with others, pleaded for the creation of a Jewish state.
Then, of course, I am sure that all members will recognize the fact that is was the Leader of the Opposition who actively lead the move to admit the newly created state of Israel to the family of nations. Canadians generally, I think, are proud that he has been recognized for those efforts.
The applause that greeted the remarks of the Prime Minister, when he extended a welcome to Mr. David Ben-Gurion, as prolonged and as sincere as any we have had in a long time in receiving a foreign visitor, indicates our admiration not only for Israel but for the great statesman who is its prime minister. Mr. David Ben-Gurion is a man of action but he is also a man of thought. Like Balfour and Smuts, he has been able to combine the qualities of the statesman with those of one who loves philosophy and learning generally. His life has been dedicated to the survival of the Jewish people. History will demonstrate that, along with Herzl and Weiszman, he is truly one of the fathers of his country, this boy who at the age of 17 left Russia to come to what he calls Zion. Mr. David Ben-Gurion is a man of the world, and he has fought for the rights of man everywhere.
The Prime Minister mentioned yesterday that he recalled with satisfaction his own visit to Israel, and I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if I may just make this personal note. The last time I saw Mr. David Ben-Gurion was in the desert, in his kibbutz, in Israel. I shall never forget the remarkable and memorable day I had with him there in 1958. So in welcoming him here today I can characterize our visitor in no better words than those used

With insight derived of wisdom, with perseverance and courage inspired by prophetic vision, guided always by the spiritual teachings of the holy Bible, he has translated the moral concepts of our ancient heritage into a humane and democratic leadership, this assuring for Israel and himself a unique and honourable place in the history of man's struggle for freedom.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF ISRAEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the national leader of the C.C.F., I am very happy to join in the words of welcome expressed by the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Essex East to Premier Ben-Gurion, who I understand was exiled by Turkey in the first world war, later came to Canada, trained in Windsor, Nova Scotia, under British guidance and later served with the British forces in the Jewish legion; who fought against evil at that time and who has been working for all that is good ever since.
Independence came to his country 13 years ago as a result of his guidance and decision. We are proud to know today that it is a democratic socialist state which has conducted a successful experiment that is no longer an experiment but a reality that really works. Except for a short period when he became a shepherd, Mr. Ben-Gurion has been a premier. A shepherd named David became a king; a premier named David became a shepherd. He is a prophet in the land of prophets. The rewarding rehabilitation program being undertaken in Israel follows the biblical instructions given in Leviticus 19:23:
And man realizing his loss, must set out to clothe the land with trees.
That great English orator, political philosopher and statesman, Edmund Burke, said:
The nerve that never relaxes, the eye that never blenches, the thought that never wanders-these are the masters of victory.
How aptly do these words apply to Premier Ben-Gurion, our guest today, the head of a state that has nourished democracy, where it has blossomed, and has caused the desert to bloom, giving new life and hope to millions.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. G. Dinsdale (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: REPORT ON PREPARATIONS FOR CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as members of parliament are aware, preparations for the resources for tomorrow conference to be held in Montreal, October 23 to October 28 next, are now well advanced. The governments of all the provinces have cooperated with the government of Canada in planning to make the conference a most significant event in the history of our country, in so far as the development of Canada's renewable resources is concerned.
Background papers form an essential basis for the conference discussions. In all, 80 such papers have been submitted. As a number of these have been written by co-authors, upwards of 100 scientists and other experts in the various resource fields have contributed to the fund of information and judgment on which conference deliberations will be founded.
As a service to parliamentarians and the press, as well as to radio and television reporters and interested organizations and individuals, the resources for tomorrow secretariat has assembled, in each of the seven sectors involved, short summaries of background papers. For each sector a resume of highlights of the papers will be prepared. This resume is, in effect, a digest of contents designed to indicate the general pattern or trend of approach by the authors to the renewable resource development problems.
The first of these completed digests pertains to the waters sector, and this document is available in both English and French. The water sector resume will be followed, in due course, by information compiled in similar form in respect of wildlife, forestry, land use, fisheries, recreation and regional development sectors.

On January 9 I forwarded to Hon. Mr. Williston, minister of lands and forests for British Columbia and chairman of the British Columbia section of the Canada-British Columbia policy liaison committee on Columbia river development, a copy of the text of the treaty which had been unanimously recommended by the Canadian and American negotiators to their respective governments. This recommendation was signed by the deputy minister of lands of British Columbia as well as by myself.
In my covering letter to Mr. Williston I advised him that it was our intention to sign the treaty on January 16 and that under all the circumstances, including the participation and signature of Mr. Bassett, his deputy minister, we assumed that the British Columbia government was in accord with the terms of the treaty unless I heard from Mr. Williston to the contrary. Mr. Williston acknowledged receipt of the copy of the text of the treaty and of the Canadian negotiator's recommendation on January 12. No suggestion was then, or ever, made that the treaty should not be signed.

(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, the impression we get from the estimates brought down by the Minister of Justice for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1962, is that of a marked increase in that department's expenditures over the past few years.
At the moment, we are called upon to vote estimates totalling $33,481,664. During the last fiscal year, the committee approved an expenditure of $28,328,287 for the same services, that is $5,153,377 less than this year. In other words, this year's estimates are slightly more than 18 per cent higher than last year's.
In 1957 when this department's estimates were examined by a special committee, parliament authorized the then minister to spend $18,615,230, namely $14,866,434 less than this year.
That means that the estimates we are asked to approve are 75 per cent higher than those voted by the house in 1957.
We would understand and agree if the increase in this year's estimates over those of 1957 were proportionate to the salary increases granted by the civil service commission, to the increase, since then, in the number of judges of the various federal courts and to the additional expenditures incurred by the implementation of certain recommendations of the Fauteux commission, like the ones concerning the national parole board, to the improvement of a few of the existing penitentiaries and the construction of a few new penitentaries.

But those items-the national parole board, the penitentiaries and the various federal courts, come under a different heading in the estimates now tabled by the minister.
If you consider the item before us, dealing with departmental administration, you find that the minister is asking the committee to vote an amount of $1,194,583, or $250,346 more than last year, an increase of close to 30 per cent.
In 1957, for the same item which was then numbered 166, the then minister asked the house to vote the amount of $513,658, or $680,925 less than what the minister is asking for now. For this item alone, the expenses anticipated by the minister for the current fiscal year are therefore 130 per cent above those incurred in 1957.
The administration of the Parole Act and the penitentiaries service show increases of $79,503 and $4,443,532 respectively, which makes a total of $4,523,035, or 20 per cent more than last year. Those two services will cost the taxpayers, for the current fiscal year, the sum of $24,687,224.
Last year, for those two services, the Department of Justice had been voted a total of $20,164,189.
In 1957, this committee had voted appropriations of $186,585 and $11,514,643 respectively for those two services, a total of $11,701,228, or less than half what we are now asked to vote.
Faced with this impressive and rapid increase in the votes asked by the Minister of Justice, we are forced to recall the criticism the Conservative party used to make when they were in the opposition and their promises to the electorate in 1957 and 1958, that, once elected, they would cut each department's expenses and would follow a policy of strict economy to reduce the taxpayer's burden.
As the elected representatives of the people it is our duty to check the use which is made of the money the people pay daily through taxes and to ask ourselves whether the people get out of this increase in government expenditures, advantages which are equivalent to the sacrifices they have to make, and, finally, whether those funds are used in accordance with the principles of efficiency and thrift we can rightly expect the government to follow.
This obligation brings us to make a closer and more accurate examination of the items included under the heading "Departmental Administration."

I now have a few brief remarks to make in regard to those who are generally called the top officials of the Department of Justice,
[Mr. Eudes.l
that is, those who enjoy the confidence of the minister and who, because of their experience and ability, are called upon to advise him in his important function. I mean, for instance, the Solicitor General, the deputy minister, the two associate deputy ministers, the two assistant deputy ministers, the executive assistants, the private secretaries, the assistant secretaries, the legal advisers, the administrative and technical officers, as well as the heads of the various branches.
Those high officials help the Minister of Justice solve the many legal issues which are submitted to him by the various other government departments.
The Minister of Justice is, in fact, the legal adviser of his cabinet colleagues and, sometimes of the provincial legislatures on these matters.
The advice of those high officials is therefore sought whenever the government intends, for instance, to amend the Criminal Code, the Bankruptcy Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act, the Patent Act, and in general, in respect of any bill submitted to parliament.
All those bills, are necessarily more or less directly connected with civil law.
However, the province of Quebec has a civil law of its own, which differs substantially from that of the other provinces, and which, needless to say, is a most highly prized part of its heritage.
I am not in any sense suggesting that those officials, in discharging their duties, fail to take cognizance of this peculiarity of the province of Quebec in their advice to the minister. However, this peculiarity logically calls for a reasonable representation, within this group of officials, of people steeped in Quebec civil law.
Last year, there was one deputy minister from the province of Quebec out of three. This year, out of five deputies, only one seems to be from the province of Quebec.
Similarly, out of five members on the national parole board, only one seems to be from the province of Quebec. The same remark applies to practically every division of the department.
It seems to me that in the discharge of such important duties, particularly in view of the complications arising from this peculiarity of Quebec civil law, the task of these officials, and hence that of the minister, would be made easier and more effective if there were a more adequate representation of people thoroughly trained in the civil law of that province.

I have just referred to the national parole board.
I am pleased-I had raised this question in the house on April 22 and June 18, 1959- that the minister has accepted the recommendations then put forward by the associations particularly interested in the rehabilitation of criminals of the female sex, to the effect that a woman be appointed to that parole board.
The female inmates in our penitentiaries, while they do not represent a large proportion of the total number of inmates, nevertheless are increasing in numbers year by year, and surely they need, with respect to both detention and rehabilitation, a treatment different from that which is applied to the male inmates.
Miss M. L. Lynch will, I have no doubt, be of effective assistance to her colleagues on that board in this particular aspect of the important social problem of rehabilitating criminals of the female sex.
Since the end of last war, especially, crime in every shape and form has been on the increase to a frightening degree in all countries and such outbreak often attended by violence has caused persons who generally remain indifferent to social problems which do not concern them personally, to revolt against it.
Public opinion has been alerted. Sociologists, moralists, criminologists, public officers, the people's elected representatives are considering the problem.
In this connection the third biennial Canadian congress of corrections was held in Toronto from May 14 to May 19 last.
That interesting meeting shows the importance being attached today to the problem raised by the criminal in society and it will be of valuable help in finding a solution.
According to the program, on Wednesday, May 17, Mr. George McLean presided over a discussion on information or communications of an administrative nature. The man is introduced in the following terms: Information Representative, Department of Justice, Canada.
But what seems strange to me, is that nowhere in the government telephone book, under any division of the Department of Justice could I find the name of that Mr. George McLean.
If he is not an employee of the Department of Justice, why was he described as

"Information Representative, Department of Justice, Canada". I wonder if the department has paid him representation expenses.
After that digression, I should like to come back to the serious and difficult problem facing society and the government, because of the increased number of crimes.
Following extensive and objective studies in several countries, it has been found that there is a tendency to consider criminals in a more humanitarian light.
Criminals are seldom considered nowadays as reprobated and repugnant human beings to whom, on account of their crimes, must be meted out exemplary punishment.
More and more the tendency is to examine criminals in their psychic and psychological behaviour, instead of merely banishing them from society.
So people wonder why, among so many human beings possessing in general the same moral and physical faculties, living in an almost identical environment, subject to the same difficulties, one of them should become guilty of an act for which the court will condemn him to reclusion for years, in a penal institution.
Personally, I think a criminal, even for his first offence, does not deserve absolution without penance. Besides, our judges, in the case of first offences, show much understanding and humanity toward the accused.
Most of the time, sentence is deferred in order to give the judge a chance to consider the accused under the circumstances which have surrounded his criminal act and his conduct up to that time, precisely in order not to punish him harshly but to impose upon him the fair punishment he deserves.

Mr. Chairman, before the house took recess, I was speaking about the upsurge in the incidence of crime and of the growing tendency to look upon the criminal from a more humanitarian angle.
In this respect, however, we must take care that our humane feelings do not lead us to

Supply-Justice
the other extreme, i.e., mawkish sentimentality. Even in the case of his first offence, the criminal must be considered as a malefactor towards his victim, though he himself may only too often be considered as a victim of society, in the widest sense of the word, for instance through lack of family education, or a deficient family education, and, therefore, because of bad examples in his family surroundings, without the necessary correctives; he may be so as a result of lack of understanding on the part of a teacher or employer, with a resulting attitude or rebellion against any authority or persons considered superior; or again he may be a victim because he cannot earn a living by his own work and according to his abilities and needs, which again is a cause of resentment against society as a whole. After he has served his sentence, the criminal tries to reinstate himself into society. It is at this point that society must play its part, accept him into its ranks, and give him employment as soon as possible. Otherwise, if he remains out of work, he will turn again to crime, convinced as he will be that he has to live outside the pale of society.
Unfortunately, it seems that, in spite of the activity of the national parole board no progress worth mentioning is apparent with regard to the rehabilitation of criminals or their reintegration into a normal life within society.
That remark is based on the last report submitted to the minister by the penitentiaries commission.
The report reveals that, on March 31, 1960, the total number of prisoners registered in the penitentiaries was 6,344. Judging by the sentences meted out every day in the courts, I think this number must have increased since.

I therefore have no doubt that following the many sentences meted out each day in our courts of justice, the number of those criminals will have increased since then. From this number we have to deduct the criminals who have avoided arrest.
The same report notes a general and steady increase, since 1956-57, in the number of admissions to penitentiaries. The St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary has set a sad and regrettable record in this respect, with an increase of 435 compared to the previous year.
A fact which makes us think and which motivated my earlier remarks is that out of this total of prisoners, 1,186, i.e., 18.69 per cent are serving a first sentence. We may therefore gather, which is more deplorable still, even if we consider the previous record, that 5,158 of all those prisoners were at that time habitual offenders, in the appalling proportion of 81.30 per cent.
During the year ending March 31, 1960, 3,403 prisoners were sent to the penitentiaries, 1,468, or 43 per cent, of them being habitual offenders.
On page 16, paragraph 47, the same report notes that the influence of the national parole board has been felt to a marked degree, for, by virtue of the parole board act, 1,427 prisoners were discharged, compared to 839 during the previous year. Now, during the same period, 1,468 habitual offenders were sent back to the penitentiary. It might therefore be interesting to know how many of the 1,427 discharged prisoners are today leading a normal life and have not, since their discharge, been brought again before the courts under some criminal charge.
Another revealing fact which may give a better idea of that dark and gloomy picture of crime, is found in paragraph 52, page 17, of the said report where is is said that 776 prisoners among the 3,403 incarcerated during the year ending March 31, 1960, were under 21 years of age, that is 23.28 per cent, which represents an increase of 124 compared to the previous year. Among those 776 inmates under 21, a total of 401 which means 50 per cent, are habitual offenders.
This completely objective examination of the criminality situation in this country, based on official statistics which do not include the number of inmates of prisons under provincial jurisdiction, warrants some serious reflection.
Not one of us, I presume, remains indifferent when, in reading his newspaper every morning, he finds the lengthy account of the crimes committed the day before.

I do not claim to know the causes of this constant rise in criminality, but while I am no specialist in the field, one can accept without fear of error the theory that the criminal is not alone responsible for his crime.
Every day we hear of accused people who, having either pleaded guilty or been found guilty, are asked by the judge "But why have you committed this crime for which I have to sentence you to so many years in prison?" And they reply: "It is because I was led to it".
Indeed, many factors can lead to crime: defective home education, bad examples from parents, bad literature or movies, the failure of society to provide means of earning a living, and on the other hand, the inexplicable ease with which one can obtain weapons, the unconcern of society and even its refusal to assist in the rehabilitation of the criminal.
I am reminded of the case of a federal civil servant who was dismissed after years of loyal and competent service, when it was discovered that some ten years before, he had been found guilty of shattering a store window with intent to steal.
As to movies, despite the constant efforts of the various organizations which, across the country, are concerned with morality and particularly with the problem of criminality, it is astonishing to see the number of pictures using as their theme either crime or gunfights.
In fact, those movies are advertised in the newspapers and on movie house billboards, with pictures always showing as the centre of attraction an actor holding a revolver in his hand. Even if those pictures do not glorify crime, they seem to revel in its detailed exposure and in showing the many uses to which firearms may be put. In many cases, they may be regarded as a kind of finishing course for budding criminals. Their suggestive pictures-we all know the influence of pictures-cannot but leave a damaging imprint on the minds of the young.
In that regard, television networks, whether of the C.B.C. or not, surely deserve no compliment. There is no doubt that close to four pictures out of five which are shown in our homes through television display a hero, good or bad, who packs a pistol.
While each one of those pictures may not be immoral in itself, the repetition of fights, battles and killings can only have a bad influence on young minds.

Thus-unconsciously perhaps, for the purpose of making money-a climate is created which gives the impression that crime is easy, less odious, and that the use of firearms is normal and practically necessary in society.

According to experts in that field, one of the main causes for the increasing number of crimes and their increased violence is the ease with which firearms can be obtained.
Without those arms, there would be practically no crime.
Mr. Justice Wilfrid Lazure, president of the court of Queen's bench, in Montreal, and a foremost authority in criminology, said that

How many other persons are legally in possession of a firearm whose necessity is highly questionable, and how many crimes would have been avoided if their author had not been in possession, even lawfully, of one of those firearms?

That question was brought up on June 30, 1959, when the Criminal Code was amended, and again last year, on June 30, 1960, when the estimates of the same department were before us.

The problem of firearms generally is a large, important, urgent but very difficult problem, and I have given instructions to my department and to the R.C.M. On Tuesday May 16, 1961, answering a question put by my colleague the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Descha-telets) concerning that matter, the Minister of Justice said:

Once released, he insisted on regaining possession of his arm which, in fact, was given back to him the following day. And it is with this very arm that a few days later he killed constable Lacombe.
The Criminal Code could perhaps include a specific provision allowing a judge, at his discretion, even if he releases a man charged with committing a crime or attempting to commit a crime with an offensive weapon, to order final confiscation of the weapon, to annul the accused's permit to carry a firearm and make it impossible for him to renew his permit.

Indeed, the seriousness of the present crime wave and the number of upheavals in penitentiaries are certainly due to the use of barbiturates.
Under present legislation, legal proceedings for the use of narcotics must be taken under chapter 201 which comes under the Department of National Health and Welfare.

The crimes listed in that chapter are of a restricted and limited nature.

The well founded representations which the Canadian consumers' association made to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and to the Minister of Justice makes you wonder.
Those trading stamps are nothing but a sham. Calculating the number of stamps he needs to get the premium, the article described in the catalogue, the consumer no longer stops to ask himself if he needs the product he is buying; his sole ambition is to collect the required number of stamps. Such practice is certainly not in keeping with the spirit of the law. It offers unfair competition to the small retailer and is an important inflationary factor in our economy.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon I should first like to thank the hon. member for Skeena, who expected to speak at this time but who allowed me to go on instead, because of another engagement I have.
Before entering into the discussion in respect of the estimates of the Department of Justice, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Hochelaga. I listened to his remarks with great care ahd can only conclude that he has made a great study of this subject, and is a man with considerable knowledge of jurisprudence.
In speaking on the estimates themselves, my first words are of praise for the Department of Justice and in particular the Minister of Justice. It is in no spirit of affectation that I say, and I think hon. members will agree, that the minister is young in years, an earnest student of jurisprudence, and a reformer. Since he has taken over the Department of Justice we have been able to consider such things as the reform of the practice of parole of prisoners-a subject which has been dealt with by the hon. member for Hochelaga-as well as reform in respect of the pensions of widows of judges, which certainly needed reviewing. We have also been able to think in

Supply-Justice
terms of legislation in respect of judges themselves, in making certain that we have a strong judiciary at all times in every province of this great country.
I also have in mind, as I am sure all hon. members have, the question of the reforming of prisoners. When lawyers have occasion to speak about this matter they think of young men from good families who through no fault of their own sometimes get into serious difficulties and are incarcerated in one of the institutions in this country. There has been a lot of reform in that regard. I also think it took a real statesman like the minister to come to grips with the subject of capital punishment. I do not want to deal with that because it is before the house in another measure. I simply wish to say that the minister has come to grips with the subject, and we have now progressed along the road in that if the bill is passed, capital punishment will be abolished with respect to certain kinds of murder.
I should like to deal with some of the matters I mentioned in my introductory remarks, and one of them is the parole board itself. I think all of us appreciate that this country is only as strong as its families. When one of our sons or daughters runs afoul of the law and is incarcerated in an institution, we want to have that son or daughter rehabilitated so they may take their place in society with other Canadians. I wish to congratulate the minister most warmly in this regard, because the emphasis has been placed on the rehabilitation of such prisoners wherever they may be incarcerated. We have set up a new parole board which reviews cases from the psychological and sociological points of view. The board takes into consideration the crime of which the person was convicted and all other circumstances; and if we can put one person back into society, if we can save one Canadian every day, we are doing a job in this particular field. I would say that the national parole board and its officials are doing an excellent job in that regard.
I should also like to mention the changed attitude with regard to penitentiaries. The old bars and cement are disappearing to some extent. We now have three types of institutions, minimum, medium and maximum security. When a person has been convicted of a first offence surely that person, as has been said many times before in the house by able jurists, should not be forced to mix with hardened criminals who need to be under maximum security. Therefore we have established a different kind of penitentiary that does not have maximum security. We have established prison farms for people of

this type, and rehabilitation starts immediately they come to such an institution. At these prison farms we have now established a person takes his place with others knowing full well that he will be assisted in rehabilitating himself to take his place in society.
Then we have medium security institutions for people who may have committed the same offence again, or are put there because other circumstances enter into the picture. Last, we have maximum security institutions for those persons who do not respond no matter what the penitentiary officials do or what judges may say. These people have come before the bar of justice many times for offences and, of course, a criminal of this type must be kept away from society until there is some sign that he is prepared to be rehabilitated. I think this reform was necessary and overdue, and I wish to congratulate the young and aggressive minister for bringing it about.
I should like to say a few words about the judges themselves. After all, I think the administration of justice really is the window dressing and the colour of democracy. Just recently I picked up an old book that belonged to my mother. The book is 100 years old, and I should like to quote a statement which represents the view of those who believe in the rule of law:
Law does not put the least restraint Upon our freedom, but maintains it;
Or, if it does, 'tis for our good,
To give us freer latitude;
For wholesome laws preserve us free,
By stinting of our liberty.
In other words, we have to give up a little of our freedom for the good of society, but out of it all we get a greater degree of freedom. As a lawyer I believe that over the years we have always had a good and independent judiciary. Not only under the present government but under the former one good appointments were made to the bench. Only two weeks ago I was before a judge who was appointed by the former administration. He is a man who was born in Alberta and whose parents came from central Europe. He was able to hand out the kind of justice that every Canadian feels should be dispensed. This is the calibre of man that we need on the bench. I think the government has seen to it that our judges have continued to be of a high calibre so that at all times in our democracy we have a judiciary of high standard which exercises great care in the application of the laws of our country.
With respect to those men who have dedicated themselves to serve as judges, I would point out that too often people say that this judge or that judge is making so many thousands of dollars a year. There is a tremendous

responsibility in accepting a judgeship in this country. Many of our top lawyers who could earn three or four times the salary of a judge by practising law make a financial sacrifice in order to assume this responsibility in our society, to see that our way of life remains free, and because they believe that the right calibre of man should sit on the bench to administer justice. When we have men of this type coming forward and making sacrifices to serve their country, I think it is up to us to make certain that their families are protected. A judge is expected to maintain a certain standard of living, and their salaries over the years have been far from commensurate with the work they do. I know of several widows of judges who have been left without the necessary security and whose pension is very low, sometimes $3,000 or less. I am glad to see that the situation is being reviewed, because if we expect these men to make the kind of sacrifices they do make in many cases when they go on the bench, the people of this country should be prepared to make certain that their families are protected and compensated for the sacrifice the head of the household has made.
With reference to judges' pensions, while it may not be true today it certainly was true in the past that men went on the bench at an early age to serve their country and were not able to save very much money before doing so. When the time of retirement came they found themselves having to reduce their standard of living considerably. I am glad to see that this matter is also being reviewed.
I want to deal now with something that concerns my own constituency. I would ask the minister to bear with me, because I have another engagement and I may not be here when the particular item is being dealt with. I feel the matter is very important to the constituency of Bow River and particularly to the Drumheller area. Hon. members have heard me mention this matter on other occasions, and I want to be fair in dealing with the circumstances. I am talking about the soft coal mines in the Drumheller area, and I will relate this matter to the estimates before us at the present time. There are two industries there. On the one hand there is a rich farming area and, on the other hand, there is a very depressed coal mining industry. Because of the competition of natural gas and petroleum with coal, miners have been thrown out of work and as a result there is a degree of unemployment in the area similar to that in Springhill.
I come now to the point. I am asking the minister and his officials to give serious consideration to the establishment of a penitentiary in the Drumheller area when a peni-

I have mentioned that it is an excellent farming area, and I have referred to the unemployment situation. Unemployment there is not something new. It occurred between the first and second wars and has happened again since the second war because of the competition of other fuels with coal. The kind of coal mined in that area is domestic fuel; therefore the industry was hard hit by the petroleum industry immediately it entered the competitive picture. These men who have put everything they have earned over the years into their little homes or their little institutions are forced to leave that area when the mines close. I say, therefore, this is a disaster area because of the relief situation. If something could be done, such as the erection of a federal institution, these men would be helped. Let us look at the attributes of the area itself. It is a large farming area. As I have said, there is a great deal of unemployment. There are good access roads, because that area has been represented by a member of the legislature who has been minister of highways for a number of years. The chamber of commerce of Alberta has asked for it. Organizations of coal workers have asked for it. In fact the people of the whole area have petitioned for it, because they have the same feeling that I am endeavouring to express in words today in respect of these people who find themselves in a very unhappy plight.

I want to refer to two or three other matters before I conclude my remarks. I promised to be brief because the hon. member for Skeena was kind enough to allow me to speak in his place, since I have to leave. At the beginning of my remarks I mentioned the importance of the administration of justice in the province of Alberta. This is the one province in which the right to a jury trial in the supreme court can be waived because of the old Northwest Territories Act which is still part of the law of the province of Alberta. I have been one of those men at the bar who think that the guilt or innocence of an accused person should be determined by a jury of his own peers. I do not say it would happen today, but there is a danger that judges may say we do not want juries, and then if defence counsel insist on juries and the accused is convicted, the sentence might be a little more severe. These are dangers that exist in an environment in which there is no jury. I suggest, as I speak for the province in that regard, that we should exercise great care when we are thinking about doing away with the jury.

Initially I should like to deal with the functions of the Minister of Justice and to say I believe he has not properly carried out his duties. feel it was a great error for parliament to enact that particular section in the bill of rights. What we did was to put into a statute a responsibility of the minister in so far as the internal functions of parliament were concerned. We were then drawing into our activities the Senate, the crown and presumably the courts.
This has been dealt with in a couple of instances in the United Kingdom, when members introduced bills dealing with the internal functions of parliament itself. It was held on a couple of occasions by Speakers in the United Kingdom parliament that it was not competent for parliament to entertain bills which contained provisions relating to the internal functions of the house itself. This is what we have done by the enactment of section 3 of the bill of rights giving the Minister of Justice a certain responsibility to examine the bills presented to parliament.

I therefore submit he has been derelict in the duty ascribed to him by this parliament under section 3 of the bill of rights. As found at page 4229 of Hansard of May 2, 1961, when the Minister of Justice was then discussing Bill No. C-86, which was the bill in the name of the Minister of Fisheries to amend the Fisheries Act, this is what the minister said:
I can assure the house that my colleague the Minister of Fisheries is, as are all members of the present government, most careful to review the legislation and the activities of the officers for which he is responsible to ensure that the legislation does not place him or his officers in a position where things are likely to be done contrary to the bill of rights.
On that occasion the minister said that Bill No. C-86 was designed to overcome the inconsistencies of the old Fisheries Act with the bill of rights. Then he pointed out further as follows, and I quote again from page 4229 of Hansard:
-we have here before us today a very concrete example of the effectiveness of the bill of rights. When you see the extent to which the Fisheries Act, a statute which has been on the books for many years, has offended the provisions of the present bill of rights, you will understand the important step forward made in introducing this piece of legislation entirely in conformity with that bill of rights.
As found on page 4230 he said further:
This government has had this under consideration since last fall, shortly after the bill of rights became effective in order to bring in legislation which will remove the objectionable features so that the officers of the Department of Fisheries, from the minister down, will be administering a piece of legislation which is in conformity with the bill of rights.
Here on three separate occasions or in three separate comments during the same day the Minister of Justice said that the old Fisheries Act to some extent was inconsistent with the bill of rights, and that Bill No. C-86 introduced by the Minister of Fisheries cleared up those inconsistencies.
We know what is contained in Bill No. C-76, in the name of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. That is a bill to re-enact the old Fisheries Act, with an additional clause that it should be studied to find out whether it is inconsistent with the bill of rights. I submit that the minister, by his own admission, has studied Bill No. C-76. By his own admission in another way he has told us that it contains a provision which is inconsistent with the

bill of rights. Yet he adamantly refuses to carry out the responsibility placed upon him by parliament and to report those inconsistencies to parliament, all because of some political embarrassment, perhaps. Regardless of the embarrassment that might be felt, I submit that the minister has no right to hide his embarrassment behind the argument that he feels Bill No. C-76 is not a bill properly before parliament, and he has been delinquent in his duties in this regard.
The bill of rights says the minister must examine and report at the first convenient opportunity. Surely the first convenient opportunity has passed in as much as it is now two months since Bill No. C-76 was introduced. Surely the first convenient opportunity has passed when the minister, by his own admission, says he has already examined the Fisheries Act and the bill introduced by the minister and found that certain inconsistencies in the old act were cleared up.
I do not want to suggest that the minister should take himself to court and sue himself under the section of the Criminal Code which deals with this question. There is a section of the Criminal Code which applies, section 107, and the minister is not above this particular section. This section says it is an offence against the Criminal Code to refuse to carry out responsibilities that a person is duty bound to carry out.
I think in this instance, Mr. Chairman, there is a prime example of a minister of the crown failing for one reason or another, or deliberately refusing to comply with a statute passed by this parliament, namely the bill of rights, to examine certain legislation and report to parliament upon it.
While we are on the subject of the examination of bills which are presented to the House of Commons may I again make reference to a question which I asked the minister concerning his activities in the field of divorce bills. On March 7, 1961, the minister was extremely busy because he examined 108 divorce bills which had been presented to this house, and he found none of them inconsistent with the bill of rights.
Let us take a look at one of the divorce bills which the minister examined and said is not inconsistent with the bill of rights. Let us take Bill No. SD-36 as an example. This is one of the bills the minister examined on March 7. Let us just see what he examined. This is the bill:
An act for the relief of Hela Hinda Fachler.
The preamble says:
Whereas Hela Hinda Fachler, residing at the city of Montreal, in the province of Quebec, wife of Szmuel (Samuel) Fachler, who is domiciled in Canada and residing at the said city, has by her petition alleged that they were married on the twenty third day of October, A.D. 1945, at the

city of Lodz, Poland, she then being Hela Hinda Chaim; and whereas by her petition she has prayed that,-
This is what the minister has examined:
-on the ground of his adultery since then, their marriage be dissolved; and whereas the said marriage and adultery have been proved by evidence adduced and it is expedient that the prayer of her petition be granted: Therefore Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
1.	The said marriage is hereby dissolved, and shall be henceforth null and void to all intents and purposes whatsoever.
The minister says this bill is not inconsistent with the bill of rights. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that it is as inconsistent with the bill of rights as anything could be. I should like to quote again from the bill of rights. Section 2 (e) provides that no law of Canada shall be construed or applied so as to:
-deprive a person of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice for the determination of his rights and obligations;
I submit that Bill No. SD-36 has deprived a person of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice for the determination of his rights and obligations.
Let us take a closer look at what occurred with regard to this particular bill. I have here a sworn affidavit and I should like to read it. It was sworn in the province of Quebec, district of Montreal, on the fourth day of May, 1960, before Mr. Morton Morris, commissioner of the superior court for the district of Montreal. It reads as follows:
I, Charles Charron, investigator, residing at No. 252 Georges Etienne Cartier Square, in the city and district of Montreal, and therein domiciled, do solemnly declare:
1.	That on the twenty sixth day of April, 1960, between the hours of five and six p.m., I did serve the corespondent Rose Franklin with a true copy of the notice hereto attached and marked "A", by giving the said copy and leaving the same with the said Rose Franklin in person, at her domicile, at No. 3145 Clarke street, in the city of Montreal, province of Quebec.
2.	That at the same time and place and in the same manner, I also served the said Rose Franklin with a true copy of the petition, hereto attached and marked "B", and a sworn declaration of the petitioner attached to the copy of the petition and also marked "B", appended to which copy there was a true copy of the information to the corespondent Rose Franklin which hereto is also attached and marked "C".
3.	That I believe that the said Rose Franklin to be the person described in the said information to the corespondent.
4.	That when serving the above upon the said Rose Franklin she admitted to me that she was the person described in the said information to be to the corespondent.
And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing it to be true and knowing that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath and by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act.
Supply-J ustice
That is signed by Charles Charron. You will note that the relevant parts of this, Mr. Chairman, are that Mr. Charron swears that he served someone by the name of Rose Franklin who is named as the corespondent in this particular case, at a particular address, 3145 Clarke street and she admitted she was Rose Franklin, the person described therein.
The only point in all this is that there is no No. 3145 Clarke street; it does not exist. If the address does not exist, how can Mr. Charles Charron swear that he served someone with a series of documents at that particular address? I submit that not only does the address 3145 Clarke street not exist, but neither does the corespondent.
Letters were mailed to Rose Franklin at 3145 Clarke street. A letter was attempted to be delivered by the postal service and I will quote from a letter received from the postal authorities in this regard:
The address of 3145 Clarke is inexistent and a directory service did not establish the present address of this Rose Franklin. The item is included.
This was after the letter was mailed to Rose Franklin at that address, after it had been returned by the Post Office Department indicating on the letter that the address did not exist, after it had then been sent back to the postal department with the request to check again and make sure that the information I just read out was correct, that the address of 3145 Clarke street was inexistent.
If the Minister of Justice says he looked at Bill No. SD-36 and at the part that says, "and whereas the said marriage and adultery have been proved by evidence adduced." without going into the evidence adduced, and came to the conclusion that this was not inconsistent with the bill of rights, what about the right of the individual, of the respondent in this case? This same gentleman, Mr. Charron, who swore that he delivered something to a woman at an address which does not exist also swears-and we are entitled to cast some doubt upon this-that he served the respondent at his particular address, and the address is given here.
I submit that Bill No. SD-36 is inconsistent with the bill of rights because it deprives a person of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice. Is it not the right of an individual who was named as a corespondent to have the opportunity of a fair hearing? And how can there be a fair hearing when there is no address at which the investigator can call or leave his papers? Our old friend Mr. Charron, whose evidence has given rise to several difficulties in the past, swore, nevertheless, that this address existed in the case to which I am referring. We are changing the status of the respondent in this case

Supply-Justice
from, that of a married person to that of a single person, without, I submit, giving him the right of a fair hearing.
This is something serious and casts a bad light upon the administration of justice in this country especially when we consider that this incident occurred within the very building which we occupy at the moment, when we consider that Mr. Charron and people like him can come before the Senate and swear affidavits to the effect that a particular address exists, when subsequently it is discovered that the address does not exist.
Let me take another case. I understand I have only a few minutes of my time left. Perhaps I should go into it on a subsequent occasion and draw to the attention of the minister another case where an individual swore on oath by affidavit that he had served a particular person with a notice at a particular address when that address does not exist, or at least, has not since 1952. We made a check on this through the legal department of the city of Montreal and we have correspondence from the city of Montreal with respect to a number of addresses which do not exist and which have never existed since 1952 according to the search which the city of Montreal made into its records. Yet in each of those instances somebody, a bailiff or an investigator, swore a statutory declaration on oath that he had served a person with copies of certain documents at the address which does not exist.
Surely this is an abuse of the efforts and of the credulity of parliament. In addition, it demonstrates how carelessly these divorce cases are dealt with and how much responsibility must fall on the shoulders of the Minister of Justice, as laid down in the bill of rights, to examine every bill to see that the rights of individuals are fully protected. Contingent upon that I say responsibility falls upon the minister to examine the evidence given before the Senate in every instance in order to ensure that this sort of hanky panky does not continue on the part of individuals such as Mr. Charron upon whose evidence grave doubts were cast, I submit, on three occasions last year.
Here again we find a certain person swearing he did a certain thing, and yet the particular address at which he was supposed to have done it does not exist. I have only mentioned this one case at this time but, as I have indicated, there are more of them, and in my opinion they should be placed on record so that they can come to the attention of those who are petitioning for these divorces, come to the attention of the persons whose names are blackened because they have been placed in categories to which they do not

necessarily belong, come to the attention of the Minister of Justice directly, so that he may have immediate knowledge of them, and, finally, come to the attention of members of the other place so that those who study these proceedings there may not be so careless in the future when they deal with these petitions. I think they should be placed on record, too, in order that the bill of rights may be carried to its full conclusion and innocent people protected to the greatest possible extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I rise at this time not because I think that what the hon. member has said is very serious-indeed, I think he himself realizes that he had his tongue in his cheek most of the time when he was saying it-but because in the course of his observations the hon. member drew a number of conclusions which, I think should not be allowed to stand isolated on the pages of Hansard. I think the true facts should be put on record so that they will appear as closely as possible to the inaccurate conclusions which were drawn by the hon. member who has just spoken.
To deal generally with the question of divorce bills, the hon. member seems to have concluded that the bill of rights requires the Minister of Justice to become a private detective rather than Minister of Justice. That was never the intention of the bill and it certainly is not the intention of the minister. If the hon. member had stopped to reflect, or if he would stop to reflect, he would himself be forced to the conclusion that there is nothing in any of these divorce bills which in itself is contrary to the bill of rights. There is nothing in any of these bills which deprives any of the persons concerned of the right to a fair hearing.
The hon. member is seeking to make an oblique and indirect attack upon the Senate divorce committee. I think it would have been open to me to have raised a point of order, but I refrained because I did not think it would have advanced the interests of this house to do so. All the hon. member has been doing is suggesting that the Senate divorce committee has not properly investigated the evidence which came before it. The hon. member read into the record of this committee an affidavit which, he said, was full of false allegations. He went on further to suggest that the Minister of Justice had somehow been negligent in not reporting that the bill to which that affidavit related was inconsistent with the bill of rights. My obligation is to examine the bill. The affidavit is not part of the bill. Therefore, the fact that I reported the bill as not being inconsistent with the provisions of the bill of rights is in no way influenced by the fact that there may be

one, two, or six or a dozen affidavits presented to the Senate committee on divorce when it is considering a bill which comes before it.
The hon. gentleman has interested himself in these divorce proceedings. He has constituted himself a private detective-quite properly, if that is what he feels his role should be. But he has every right to bring before the private bills committee of this house any evidence he has that the affidavits presented in the other place are not in accordance with the facts. My obligation is to examine the bill and to report whether or not it is consistent with the provisions of the bill of rights, and not one of these multitudinous divorce bills-bills which, incidentally, are each checked in the department; it is not a routine check; every one of them is considered-is in conflict with the relevant provision of the bill of rights. The hon. member's approach has simply been to try to draw the Minister of Justice and the Department of Justice into his private vendetta with the Senate divorce committee. Into that vendetta we refuse to be drawn.
More important, although even less accurate, is the hon. member's allegation that I have been negligent in my duty under the bill of rights with regard to Bill No. C-76, which is the bill introduced by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo purportedly to amend the Fisheries Act. First I should remind Your Honour that the hon. member for Skeena said the Minister of Justice, if I recall his words correctly, had been in direct and deliberate violation of his duties under the bill of rights. The bill of rights imposes upon the minister the obligation to examine every bill introduced or presented to the House of Commons in order to ascertain whether any of the provisions therein are inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of that part of the bill of rights, and requires that the minister shall report any such inconsistencies to the House of Commons at the first convenient opportunity.
The hon. member has read certain questions and answers that were exchanged between himself and myself subsequent to the time when the bill was introduced. Those questions and answers make it perfectly clear, in my opinion, that Bill No. C-76 is not properly before the house.
I submit to you, sir, that it is my duty only to report in respect of bills that are properly before the house. It was not the intention of the bill of rights to enable an hon. member to obtain a legal opinion from the Minister of Justice in respect of an existing statute by a device which misleads the house.
Supply-Justice
Would the hon. minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The fact of the matter is that the question of whether Bill No. C-76 is properly before the house is still under discussion by the house leader and his honour, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We passed it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That matter has, therefore, not been determined.
The hon. member for Skeena has suggested that the Minister of Justice must report any inconsistencies to the house at the first convenient opportunity. I should, therefore, suggest there are two questions invilved. First, is the bill properly before the house and, second, when is the first convenient opportunity of reporting inconsistencies?
May I remind the committee that when the bill was introduced, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo said, as reported at page 3217 of Hansard for March 22, 1961 as follows:
-the purpose of this bill is to revise the Fisheries Act to bring it into conformity with the Canadian bill of rights and in accordance with the report to be tabled by the Minister of Justice under standing order 40, as required by the Canadian bill of rights regulations.
More specifically, the purpose is to determine whether the clauses which empower a fisheries officer (1) to accuse a person of violating fisheries laws, (2) to adjudicate on that person's guilt or innocence, (3) to confiscate without a hearing the property of persons, boats, fishing gear and fish, and which deny an appeal to the courts or to the Minister of Fisheries for restitution of the confiscated property if the confiscation is not coupled with a criminal charge, are consistent with the Canadian bill of rights.
When one looks at Bill No. C-76 and reads the motion of the hon. member, one will realize that it was represented to the house, when introduced, as a bill to revise the Fisheries Act, to bring it into conformity with the bill of rights, and it was on that basis that leave to introduce the bill was given. It was also on that basis that the bill was read the first time and distributed. When we examine the bill we find it is not a bill to revise the Fisheries Act to bring it into conformity with the bill of rights, but is a bill to re-enact the Fisheries Act.
As I have explained, this is, in my view, an abuse of the legislative processes of parliament and in my submission, which I made to his honour, Mr. Speaker, the bill is not properly before the house; first, because leave to introduce it was obtained by a subterfuge, and second, because it is-I have no doubt about this point-a bill which simply reenacts the provisions of an existing statute, and is, in no jot or tittle, different from the existing statute already on the books with the exception that, at the end of the bill,

Supply-J ustice
there is a clause saying that the existing statute is repealed. It is, therefore, not a bill at all, nor a legislative process. It accomplishes nothing. How can one solemnly ask the House of Commons to entertain the proposition that it should go through all the legislative processes of first reading, second reading, committee stage and third reading, simply to re-enact something which exists already? That is an absurdity, a monstrosity, and an abuse of the processes of parliament. My view is that, as Minister of Justice, I should not lend myself to such a process. That is my answer in respect of the first question, as to whether indeed this bill is properly before parliament.
The second question is, when is the first convenient opportunity at which the minister should report to parliament in respect of any inconsistency? As I have said, I have taken up the question with his honour, Mr. Speaker, as to whether this bill is properly before parliament and, at the moment, it appears to be his honour's view that the time to raise the question is when, and if, the bill should be called for second reading. Should the hon. member attempt to proceed with this solemn farce, then most certainly a point of order should be raised as to whether this bill is properly before parliament, and at that time I should properly present my views. If it were ruled that it was properly before parliament, then, of course, it would be incumbent upon me to express my view as Minister of Justice, and I should do so without hesitation.
In the interim I suggest that the proper position is that the Minister of Justice should not be asked to do that which the bill of rights never intended him to do-express legal opinions in respect of existing statutes, on the basis of a bill introduced, by a subterfuge and misinformation, to the house. The Minister of Justice, in my opinion, would be expressing an opinion as to whether a bill is inconsistent with the bill of rights when, in my view, it is not properly before the house.
Therefore, I suggest, Mr. Chairman, there is nothing to the point raised by the hon. member for Skeena, and that in the interim the government acted, as it had intended all along, following a study of the Fisheries Act, by taking the appropriate, open and honest course in introducing its bill to revise the Fisheries Act, in order to remove those portions of that act which, upon review, were found to be inconsistent with the bill of rights. That has been done, and my opinion of the bill, presented by the Minister of Fisheries, was given in the course of the discussion in respect of that bill. I submit now that I have complied, as Minister of Justice, not

only to the letter, but to the spirit of the bill of rights and, in so doing, have avoided compounding an abuse of the parliamentary processes.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to discuss a matter in connection with the administration of justice in respect of an impropriety which probably exists to a very limited degree.
I hold all judges, appointed by this parliament, in very high regard, and believe their decisions are as impartial as they can be, and the judges are beyond the realm of politics. I also hold in high regard those individuals appointed by our provincial governments to administer the law in our junior courts. I do not know of any one of them who is, or has been, partial in his duties. However, I do not think any of them should take an active part in an election, nor should they take any direct or indirect part in the patronage which might flow from an election. An infringement of the Canada Elections Act can occur; in fact, it often does occur. I do not suggest and I have no right to suggest that they would be other than impartial but yet I would think that their decision might be suspect. This would do nothing to enhance in the minds of the people the view that the administration of justice in Canada is always impartial. It occurs to me that anyone who is strongly partisan by act or deed and who has to do with the administration of justice may be acting quite legally within the law but not with propriety under the law.
As a member of another profession, I do not propose to lecture members of the legal profession. I am referring only to those who have something to do with the administration of justice. I am as interested as any other Canadian in seeing that the administration of justice is always above reproach. In bringing this matter before the committee may I say that I quite realize that these appointments are made by the provincial governments and therefore the matter is outside the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice. However, the Criminal Code is a federal statute and we should all be interested in seeing that it is applied impartially.
After all, many more people come in contact with the junior courts than with the senior courts and their opinion about the administration of justice is formed from their experience in these junior courts. I do not bring up this matter in a partisan way and I hope the minister will not regard it as such. As I have said, the condition probably exists only to a very limited degree. I do not know whether it existed under the former government. Frankly, I have no information

on the matter but if it did exist I think it was wrong then just as I think it is wrong now.
I am not complaining because of any partisan action against our party on the part of the presiding officer of a court of lower jurisdiction. I am appealing to all Canadians to maintain the administration of justice on a high plane and above reproach. I do not suggest there should be any change with regard to the exercise of the franchise by these people although this is denied to the judges of our senior courts. I do not suggest that anything that has been done is illegal.
Would the hon. member permit a question? Would he tell us what he means by junior courts? Does he mean magistrates' courts?
I refer to magistrates' courts.
Or family courts?

Magistrates' courts. I should like the minister to reply and I should like to hear the opinions of other members of the committee. If I am wrong in my thinking I should like to be corrected. I have always thought that this practice should not be carried on and I should like to hear the opinions of other members of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, of course I would deplore any partisanship in any court, and I am glad to say that so far as I know there is no partisanship in any of the courts, certainly not those presided over by judges who are appointed under the authority of parliament. Mind you, all of us who practice in the courts and occasionally lose cases may be tempted, I suppose, to ascribe reasons, but I am satisfied it is correct to say that on the whole the bar and the public of Canada are well served indeed by their judiciary, whether it be in the superior courts of the province, county or district courts or in magistrates' courts.
The hon. member has brought before the committee a general proposition that justice should be administered without partisanship or favour, and with his proposition we would, of course, all agree. He said, however, that the situation he has in mind exists primarily with respect to magistrates' courts. He did not identify the situation. If it is in a magistrate's court, if there should be any such unidentified situation, all I can say is that it seems to me that the matter should be taken up with the authority responsible for the appointment to the magistrate's court.

I should like to make a comment at this point. I have had some experience in this connection. I was brought before a
Supply-Justice
magistrate who was a member of the legislature who was of a different political persuasion from myself. He found me guilty with a great deal of relish and ordered me to pay a certain sum. I told him to go to hell, and that I would not pay the sum in question, and I have never paid it yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The question there likely was, was the hon. member really guilty or not? I am glad to say that those bad old days in British Columbia are at an end. Even though the government of the province is not now one to whose political doctrine I subscribe, those bad old days are pretty well gone, and generally speaking that type of magistrate does not exist in our province.

I did not mean to bring about a general discussion. I happen to know of one or two cases where this does occur, where magistrates do take part in federal elections. I have never made inquiries to ascertain whether or not the practice is general but if it is I think it is wrong. I think most hon. members would agree with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sure they do, and if the hon. member would bring such a case to the attention of the provincial attorney general it is a matter upon which effective action should be taken right away.

Would the minister not agree that if it is apparent that there is the possibility of bias because of political partisanship any litigant has the right to apply for prohibition to prevent his case being heard by the particular magistrate?
I would not care to give a snap decision on that point. I should like to reflect on it a little.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have the estimates of the Department of Justice before us again. Its operations are very important to everyone but in some respects they remind me of the expression "Jefferies is chicken" used in the press gallery. It seems to me that the department acts in somewhat the same manner. The minister has referred to his obligation under the bill of rights and in that regard I should like to refer to divorce bills. Anyone who has read a divorce bill knows that it contains a petition. There is an allegation that adultery has been committed. Evidence is submitted to support the petition and a decision is made on that basis. I think the bill of rights gives the parties involved in a divorce bill a protection they are not getting at the present time from the examination that the minister gives these bills. Because of the problems that have arisen over the past few years in relation to the divorce law administered by the federal government

Supply-Justice
and the responsibility of the federal government except in those instances where jurisdiction is given to the provincial governments, it seems to me that some change must be made so that some of these things do not happen. The minister will debate, and can debate, his responsibility in relation to this matter of divorce. However, Mr. Chairman, the committee will be aware of the fact that a number of cases have been referred to the minister by the miscellaneous private bills committee and we have never received any answer.
One of these cases was the Eccles case of last year which received a great deal of publicity in the newspapers and other media of publicity across the country. To date, we have not found out the ultimate disposition of this case. We were told that the occurrence was within the jurisdiction of the provincial government, but since the occurrence took place within this building I doubt that that would be the case. Even so, there must be some follow up as to what the decision in that case was. The province of Ontario itself has gotten into a great deal of grief in this field, but at the moment inquiries are being conducted across the province in an effort to solve the problem.
I offered to help the minister this year by suggesting the setting up of a parliamentary proctor, a Queen's proctor, to do the job of making inquiries about divorce cases when that course seemed to be necessary. We have done some work in this connection and I think the minister is going to have to do some work or take some responsibility in connection with this subject. It is quite true that, technically, the minister reads the divorce bill and sees nothing wrong with the bill. This is obviously the case because there is nothing in it except the petition; there is nothing in it to prove whether or not the people involved are being given any of the protection they should expect under the bill of rights.
By May 9, 1961, the hon. member for Skeena and I had sent letters to 242 persons involved in divorce cases. Actually, as you can see, there would be 484 people who received letters in this regard. Of this number, 114 letters were returned to us for these reasons: No such street, number or person in Montreal, and for respondents there were two, for corespondents five; not in the directory, unknown, 19 respondents and 45 corespondents; moved, not at that address, 16 respondents and 18 corespondents-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I regret that I must rise on a point of order here, Mr. Chairman. I do not think it can be said of me that I am unprepared to discuss anything which is within my responsibility and to give a good deal of latitude in that connection. However,

it does seem to me that what is being done here by certain hon. members is to seek to avail themselves of the opportunity of these estimates to discuss and to criticize proceedings before the divorce committee of the Senate, and to attempt to make a case-which may be right or wrong, I do not know, because it is not within my jurisdiction-that the committee has been careless or has been misled or whatever may be the case.
In my submission, sir, this does not fall within the responsibility of the Minister of Justice in any way whatever and should not be discussed on these estimates.

I should like to speak to the point of order, Mr. Chairman. You will recall that last session the miscellaneous private bills committee reheard a particular divorce case referred to as the Eccles case. This case was referred to the Minister of Justice, and he took certain action in respect of it. We have inquired of the Minister of Justice on three separate occasions on orders of the day as to what was happening to that particular inquiry. As a result of that referral to him, he gave pertinent information as to what he had done about the case and what was happening. Recently, the minister was sent a copy of an affidavit, both from myself and I gather from the chairman of the Senate divorce committee regarding certain alleged improprieties in connection with a particular divorce case. In reply, the Minister of Justice wrote me on March 30, as follows:
Dear Mr. Howard:
Thank you very much for your letter of February 28 concerning alleged irregularities with respect to the proceedings before the Senate committee on divorce on the petition of Yvette Dubois Leduc for a bill of divorce from Jacques Leduc.
I received the original of Mrs. Barriere's letter from the chairman, Senate divorce committee, and by letter dated March 13th I informed him that I was having an investigation undertaken immediately.
In both of these instances, the minister accepted some responsibility and took steps to deal with the cases. I submit that, surely this is something within the competence of the Minister of Justice. By his own admission in the letter of March 30, he was undertaking an investigation, just as he had in respect of the Eccles case. His answers on three separate occasions indicating that certain courses of action were being taken were an acceptance of some responsibility in the field.

speechtext:
