As I was starting to explain, there is no act concerning divorce in general. This house as well as the other place pass certain divorce bills but each bill is a separate case. The Minister of Justice has nothing to do with the procedure of the other place and of this place concerning the enactment of these bills. This is the responsibility of parliament as a whole and not the special responsibility of the minister.
Although it may not be wise on my part to give an opinion in advance on the point which the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont said he wanted to raise later on, I think generally that what I have said would apply. There may be certain circumstances where one could discuss the opportunity for the government to introduce some legislation in the matter of divorce but that would not be the responsibility of the minister. It would be the responsibility of the government to introduce legislation of that kind. It would therefore not come under the estimates of the Department of Justice.
The hon. member mentioned that the British North America Act gives the federal government power to legislate in the matter of divorce and marriage. I would point out that this authority is not given to the government but to parliament. That is why a distinction must be made between the responsibility of parliament and the responsibility of the minister. That is why I do not think the minister can reply to any problem raised on the general policy of divorce. This is a problem for parliament; it is not a problem for the minister. That is why I indicated that the discussion up to the present time has been out of order when referring to the procedure which is followed in the other place or here in connection with divorce.
As to the other point raised by the hon. member for Skeena with regard to certain cases to which he drew the attention of the minister last year, may I say this. He must remember that the enforcement of the law is a provincial responsibility. It may well be that the minister will wish to co-operate when certain facts are drawn to his attention by reporting to the attorney general of the province concerned; but that will not give the minister authority or jurisdiction on this matter under his estimates. Again it is a problem for parliament but I think it is not a problem for the Minister of Justice.

Before we proceed, Mr. Chairman, may I say this. The initial raising of the objection by the Minister of Justice and the subsequent discussion in my opinion raised three other matters which should be considered before we finally determine where we stand on this particular issue. The first one
FThe Chairman.]
is this. If the administration of justice is a matter of provincial responsibility, then I submit that the Minister of Justice had no right whatsoever even to receive a communication from the miscellaneous private bills committee of last year with respect to the possibility of perjury or collusion in a particular case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: How can I avoid receiving a communication? I must open the letter. I cannot send it back unopened. Don't be so ridiculous.

speechtext: The hon. member himself sent me a communication.

The only relationship it might have is through the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Justice is the person with whom the miscellaneous private bills committee deals.

Surely we are entitled then to discuss the subject of divorce in so far as it is concerned in the Yukon territory if this is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice.

I think that on all counts we are entitled to proceed on this course in dealing with these particular items. The minister has said he examined all these various divorce bills and found them consistent with the bill of rights, and I think we are entitled to review his examination and see whether or not he is correct.

May I assist in this matter by saying that we have considered this very carefully and we have come to the conclusion that where a possible offence is brought to my attention concerning perjury alleged to have been committed in Quebec or an offence in connection with a false affidavit, then it should be brought to the attention of the Attorney General of Quebec. for the Attorney General of Canada to prosecute under the Criminal Code of Canada in the case of ordinary Criminal Code offences committed within a province. When the minister was replying to the hon. member for Skeena he made some reference to myself which I cannot allow to go unanswered. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I only hope you won't do it again.

speechtext: Except for this one case.

You keep quiet. You have had your say and I am going to have mine. Let us take this question of subterfuge. No bill can come before the house unless it complies with certain rules. If the rules have been complied with there can be no basis for a charge of subterfuge and the minister himself is lowering his dignity by suggesting it.
Let us look at the facts and not at the smokescreen which the minister has tried

Supply-Justice
to throw up. The rules governing the introduction of bills in this house are clear, and in addition we have standing orders applying with similar force to this procedure. Standing order 71, section 2, provides that a motion for leave to introduce a bill shall be decided without debate or amendment provided that any member moving for such leave may be permitted to give a succinct explanation of the provisions of the bill.
The practice which has been followed in introducing this bill is set forth in the fourth edition of Bourinot at page 494, where the following words are found:
When the two days' notice has been given, the member in charge of a public bill rises as soon as motions for the introduction of bills are called, in the course of routine proceedings, and moves formally for "leave to introduce a bill, intituled, etc." He sends to the Speaker the motion in writing with a copy of the bill. The Speaker will then propose the question. "Is it the pleasure of the house that the honourable member has leave to introduce his bill?" But if the Speaker finds that the bill is "in blank or in an imperfect shape" he will decline to put the question and will return the bill to the member who must take another opportunity of bringing it up in conformity with the rules.
Standing order 71(1) provides that every bill must be introduced by leave with the title of the bill specified. Standing order 72 provides that no bill may be introduced in blank or in an imperfect shape.
Mr. Chairman, Bourinot provides that two days' notice must be given. I submitted my bill to the Speaker 48 hours before it was introduced in the house for the purpose of having the Speaker determine whether it conformed with the rules, and whether it was in blank or in imperfect shape. I was not informed that there was anything wrong with it, and naturally concluded that I was entitled to proceed with the bill. I suggest, therefore, the minister's charge of subterfuge breaks down in respect of Bourinot's citation, that 48 hours' notice be given, because it was duly given. I suggest the minister should eat the word "subterfuge".
In respect to his suggestion that it was misleading, the purpose of the bill was explained on the blank page opposite clause 1 of the bill, which was to determine whether it was consistent with the bill of rights and to re-enact it in conformity with a report which the minister is obliged to make pursuant to the Canadian bill of rights examination regulations.

made to the legislation which is passed by the house? The minister talks about a farce; I suggest that is the biggest farce of all. It is a custom in this house which has arisen out of the rules, and has been sanctioned, that when an hon. member asks for leave to introduce a bill, he may be asked to give an explanation.
Now, the introduction of a bill, of course, has in itself no effect. The only thing that has effect is when a bill is read formally the first, second and third time. But our custom has grown that when a member is asked for an explanation so as to allow the members of the house to form a judgment on whether he may have leave to introduce the bill, because it is only when leave is given to introduce the bill that it can be read a first, second and third time. First reading is given a bill under our rules immediately upon leave for the introduction of the bill being granted. It is important, therefore, whether or not a member gets leave to introduce a bill.
While it has rarely, if ever happened, the house is quite entitled to refuse leave to introduce a bill. Certainly, if the house felt that an explanation given of a bill made the bill repugnant, the house would not give leave for the introduction of the bill. Certainly if the house were given an explanation which, on its face, raised a serious question as to whether or not the house should give the bill first reading, then the house would say, no, we will not give first reading now. We will wait until we see a copy of the bill or until we get a further explanation. Then, we would defer first reading and the bill would not have, in fact, been read a first time. I say, therefore, the explanation given by a member when he seeks leave to introduce his bill is a very important thing.
In this case, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo did explain his Bill No. C-76 on March 22, 1961. Here is what he said, as recorded on page 3217 of Hansard of that date:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to revise the Fisheries Act to bring it into conformity with the Canadian Bill of Rights and in accordance with the report to be tabled by the Minister of Justice under standing order No. 40, as required by the Canadian Bill of Rights regulations.

It was on that basis, Mr. Chairman, that the house gave leave to the hon. member to introduce the bill to revise the Fisheries Act and bring it into conformity with the bill of rights. Leave was given, the bill was introduced and it was then read a first time

I ask how anything could be a clearer case of the house having been misled?
I am not discussing motives, I am simply asking the house to assess the fact of whether or not it was misled by the explanation given. It accomplishes nothing. It was for this reason I said the bill was introduced by subterfuge. It was introduced as a result of an explanation which evaded the issue and led hon. members to believe that they were being asked to give leave to introduce a bill to revise the Fisheries Act, whereas they were being asked to give leave to introduce another, different kind of bill.

It had been my intention to rise this evening merely to comment on the impressive program initiated by the Minister of Justice in the field of penal reform, but I cannot let pass the remarks which have just been made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont. This great humanitarian who, I notice, voted against the bill which was presented to the house yesterday, presumably because he did not think the application of the death penalty should be limited, in a burst of compassion this evening decided that he wants to extend to human beings the same methods that this house voted to provide for the slaughter of animals a few years ago. I must say I am unimpressed by this sudden concern. The hon. member also made reference to special committees and I think if I were in his party I, too, would want to send out for a lot of experts and a lot of help. It is obviously a continuing process over there-
We would not call on you, I am sure.

It seems to me that the members of this house are perfectly capable of processing this bill, as they have proved capable of processing other measures and bills over the years.
Coming back, now, to my original purpose in rising this evening, I want to discuss the impressive program of penal reform which is being carried on by the present administration under the guidance of the Minister of Justice. I had the opportunity to examine some of our penal institutions at first hand not too many months ago. I had occasion to visit the city of Kingston and Queen's University and I took advantage, while I was in that city, of the opportunity to visit two institutions, the Joyceville medium security institution just outside the city, and that great monument to the reform instincts of the Liberal party, the women's prison in Kingston.
I should like to tell members something of my experience in visiting first the Joyceville institution, the medium security institution containing prisoners carefully selected as being prisoners who are deemed to be the best risk and to offer the greatest opportunity for reform and rehabilitation. This, as I say, is a medium security institution. The degree of control on the part of the guards is roughly equivalent to that of a foreman in charge of a work gang. In effect the work gangs, or work groups, were, when I saw them, leaving through the open front door of the institution and proceeding down to the side of the highway, highway No. 15, I think it is, which passes by the gate, on their way to perform various tasks connected with the prison farm, bush clearing and other outdoor activities. The institution itself is obviously adequately staffed, and supervision is as strict as it has to be. The point is that some individuals of very substantial size were wandering about in relative freedom to pursue their tasks. They were putting in a full working day and within the prison itself the main endeavour was to provide to many of the prisoners who had little or no useful experience in earning a living, the opportunity to learn a trade, to operate machine shops, tailoring shops and so on. Here is a forward looking, progressive policy in practice, and it makes so much sense that there is little serious area for criticism.
The contrast between this medium security institution and the women's institution in Kingston is, to say the least, striking. At Joyceville I had seen a burly 200 pounder walking through an open gate. At Kingston there were endless barricades, walls 40 feet high fortified with barbed wire, oak doors and bars in series, bars strong enough to resist the charge of a herd of elephants, all to be passed through before one encounters a
Supply-Justice
woman prisoner who would not have weighed more than 100 pounds soaking wet. The contrast between the open door and the animal cage was striking.
The person presently in charge of that institution was reluctant that I should visit the institution, and after I had completed my visit I could understand why. She had recently taken over the institution and was in the process of initiating some very constructive and effective measures. She was reluctant to allow me to inspect the buildings because she was in the midst of effecting these changes, and felt that if my visit was deferred two or three months, she would then be able to impress me with the efficiency and effectiveness of the operation. While I appreciate the feelings of that lady, I am pleased I had the opportunity at that time of seeing exactly what the situation was. There was, at that time, enough evidence of the previous arrangement remaining to impress me with the hopelessness of the situation as it existed before the introduction of these new methods, effected by that enlightened lady under this present administration.
There used to be at that institution a school to teach the inmates hairdressing. The female inmates were being taught how to earn an honest living at some considerable expense and effort. This school was finally discontinued because graduates, when they applied for jobs upon their release, although qualified, were refused.
I am pleased to say that, with the opening of the new building, there are now classes held in special rooms designed and equipped to teach the inmates different trades. It is my considered opinion that the old arrangement, which was an exercise in futility, has been replaced by a productive and beneficial arrangement whereby the inmates are able to learn typing, shorthand, bookkeeping, accounting and the like, and upon discharge are able to be placed in good positions. Classes in academic education also take place now at this institution in an attempt to bring the average education of the inmates up to a grade 6 level.
I should also like to mention that there is a laundry operating in the institution which has, over the years, looked after the laundry needs of the institution itself as well as neighbouring men's institutions and which worked a four hour day. Obviously this is an appropriate occupation for women prisoners but I wonder about the effectiveness of having the prisoners work only a four hour day in terms of preparing them for useful occupations after release. There is also a shirt factory in the institution which worked on the basis of a four hour day. Women who have worked there and who upon release sought employment in

Supply-Justice
shirt factories found themselves unable to sustain the pace of working an industrial eight hour day, after having worked a four hour day for four or five years. As a matter of record, very few have been able to hold their jobs after release. It is my understanding that the inmates only put in a four hour day because the guards were required to escort them from the laundry room to the mess room, to the laundry, and back to their cells. These guards worked only until 5 o'clock in the evening so the inmates had to be returned to their cells before that hour. Apparently the thought of the guards working shifts had never occurred to the officials of that institution, so that a normal seven or eight hour working day could be carried out.
If such a procedure had been followed, perhaps those inmates would have become accustomed to working a long day, and thereby would not have been faced with the sudden change upon their successful placement in a laundry in the outside world. Had this been so, at least some of them might have survived the difficulties of the transitional period from imprisonment to private life. It is unfortunate, though true, that in most cases, inmates released and placed in jobs outside met with unhappy results. I should in all fairness say, with the new programs being instituted in these institutions, the results are much better. I understand there is very little resistance to the increase in the length of the working day, although resistance was anticipated.
I have related some of my impressions of the operation and success thereof, which I found on my visit to this institution. I could take up more time in describing what I term, quite fairly, the dungeon conditions which I found there, such as one basement room in which there was a puddle of water surrounded by 20 or 30 beds. I suggest the existence of those conditions is the reason why the lady, to whom I referred earlier, was so reluctant to let me inspect the institution. However, as I say, the institution was in the midst of a change-over period, and conditions are now much improved. I was very impressed by the before and after picture.
It is quite clear that for at least a quarter of a century, perhaps more, the conditions existing in institutions in this country were completely ignored. I am happy to say that a new program is being carried out with vigour and interest, initiated by the present Minister of Justice and carried out by the officials of the penal institutions that come within federal jurisdiction. This program has had a dramatic impact, particularly in view of the difficulties which were encountered at the commencement of the program.
[Mr. McGee.1
The subject of penal reform has been discussed in this house, as well as by a number of interested individuals outside this house. It was discussed just recently during the debate on capital punishment. I have often heard statements made by uninformed individuals which would have lead me to believe, had I not known better, that a sentence of life imprisonment in these institutions could be likened to a vacation in Florida. That, of course, is not the case. The present program initiated by the Minister of Justice was embarked upon in a constructive way, in an attempt to train the inmates of these institutions, so that upon their release they would be capable of being placed in society in respectable positions and occupations. A great deal of careful planning and thought has gone into the designing of this program. I think the philosophy behind the project is sound, and that the pattern now being developed is desirable. These programs, plans and policies, however, are only as good, in the final analysis, as the results-the placing of released inmates in gainful and productive forms of employment.
I note an increase in this year's estimates of some $17,000, bringing the total to $167,500 in the form of grants to after-care agencies. The vanguard in this respect is composed, of course, of the John Howard and Elizabeth Fry societies, which are doing an outstanding job in this field. But, as I said before, Mr. Chairman, the work being done, the effort being made, the care and time taken, go for nought if upon release society in effect slams the door in the face of these individuals. This problem is, of course, aggravated in time of economic recession and, I suppose, according to the season of the year when release takes place. I think it behooves us as members of parliament, regardless of political party, to act within our capacities as ambassadors for the minister's programs and the programs instituted by these after-care organizations. If the first few doors are slammed in the face of the released inmate, we are simply and obviously increasing the possibility of recidivism, of having the released prisoner back in our institutions.
Finally, I think the most impressive feature of the minister's program of penal reform is that not only does it make sense but it actually saves the taxpayers, you and I, Mr. Chairman, money in the long run. This can be and has been demonstrated to be a fact from the point of view of cost to the state itself.
I hope that at some time during consideration of the minister's estimates he will shed further light on the question of life imprisonment and the implications thereof. There is a theory abroad, erroneous, I believe, and I

hope the minister will confirm me in my belief, that the frothing, foaming criminal guilty of a murder or a series of murders, who is found guilty and sentenced to life imprisonment, will be invited, if not encouraged, in a relatively few years to come back into society. Quite understandably fear has been expressed by members of the house and persons throughout the country that men of this type would be virtually invited to go free to kill again.
From the information I have gained in other quarters it is my impression that in our institutions at the present time there are persons who are serving sentences of life imprisonment and that for all practical purposes the sentence will be just that, life imprisonment. I say "for all practical purposes" because it seems to me that, in terms of the threat to society and the safety of society, when the person is aged, infirm and sick, literally not strong enough to harm himself let alone anyone else, there is no useful purpose in extracting the full sentence of life imprisonment and keeping such a person in hospital behind bars rather than in hospital on the other side of the bars. I hope the minister will clarify that matter for me and for the fairly large section of the public who, I believe, are under an erroneous impression concerning the effect of life imprisonment. As I said before, it is my belief that the person who clearly represents a threat to society or a likely threat to society if released simply is not released. Finally, Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate the minister on the part of the program I have followed with interest and examined at first hand and at the same time to wish him well in his future activities in this field.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I noted with interest that the hon. member for York-Scar-borough was interested primarily in the penitentiary program and, indeed, he discussed some aspects thereof. As I indicated to the committee at the commencement of discussion of my estimates today, it is my intention to make a general statement by way of a progress report on our correction and reform program when we reach the penitentiary item, and I would hope, therefore, that we might have a discussion of this matter on that item. Since it appears to me to be the fact that members are beginning to turn their attention to that matter, possibly they might be prepared to conclude the general discussion on the first item and perhaps it might be timely if I were to reply now to some of the remarks that have been made on that item so that we can proceed with the specific items in the estimates.
Supply-J ustice
The hon. member for Hochelaga commenced his remarks by drawing attention to the fact that there is an appreciable increase in the expenditure we are asking for this year compared with 1957, and there is no doubt that he is correct in drawing attention to that fact. I would, however, draw to his attention, and to the attention of the other members of the committee, that the main increase in expenditure consists primarily of the increase in the penitentiaries branch, the parole board and the salaries of the officers of the department, the penitentiaries branch and the other administrative boards that are under the general heading of the Department of Justice.
With respect to salaries, I point out that there have been two increases authorized by the civil service commission and approved by the government since 1957, that is, since the date with which the hon. member was making his comparison. I would draw his attention particularly to the fact that this increase in total expenditure by no means indicates that we are getting less value for the money that is being spent. Indeed, in my submission, we are getting more value. I would, for instance, direct his attention to the fact that under the penitentiaries branch-I am not going to discuss this in particular but this is an illustration of what I have in mind-the item for administration this year is $14,912 less than it was last year although the penitentiaries branch is spending more money this year than last year under such items as construction and maintenance. This is the pattern we have endeavoured, I believe successfully, to institute in the department.
There are certain things which are recognized as uncontrollable expenditures. If you have an increase in salaries authorized, then your salary item goes up. If you have an increase in your over-all activities, if you have a program which has the general approval and support of the house and the country and on which you must spend more money than previously, your estimates are going to reflect that increase.
The fact of the matter is that although the program has increased very considerably the proportionate amount being spent for administration has, as in the case of the penitentiaries branch, generally speaking been reduced, so that the country is getting better value for the money in part because the program is sounder than was the case before. One of the reasons why the over-all expenditure of the department has increased is, of course, that under this department there are being performed functions and activities which were not being carried out before. I have referred to the establishment of the national parole board, and I refer also to the new correctional reform program. Both

Supply-Justice
of these represent programs for which the country had had a very real need over the past years but which were not implemented until within the last two or three years.
Then, the hon. member referred to the increase in the number of legal officers, senior advisory counsel, and so on, within the department. I think the committee might be interested to know that the Department of Justice services the whole of the government of Canada, services all the departments. This work, of course, includes legal advice and counsel offered by the minister to his colleagues in the cabinet, opinions given by my deputy minister to the administrative heads of departments, assistance in particular matters given by my officers to their opposite numbers in other departments, litigation conducted on behalf of the government of Canada, the work of the criminal law section, which has responsibility for the general supervision of the Criminal Code, and those fields in which the federal government must take action under that code, and includes the legislation section, which is charged with the responsibility of the drafting of bills which are submitted by the government to this house. All of this work that I have mentioned, and much work that I have not mentioned, is carried on for the government of Canada with a total staff of 40 legal officers.
I think that if the committee will stop to reflect for a moment on the volume of work that must be done by the Department of Justice for the government of Canada, which means the people of Canada, they will realize that a staff of 40 legal officers is a very reasonable staff indeed with which to carry on that work. This number includes all the legal officers in the department from the deputy minister down. It is quite true that there has been a relatively modest increase in the number of legal officers employed by the department since 1957. One reason for this is that we have adopted, as a conscious policy, the practice of conducting more litigation, actually having the prosecution of more cases in the courts by our officers, rather than employing outside counsel.
I am not suggesting for a moment that we have adopted the practice of employing no outside counsel. We still retain and will continue to retain large numbers of outside counsel as agents of the Department of Justice in that litigation. We are, especially in certain fields, and I am thinking particularly here of important taxation cases as well as constitutional cases, endeavouring to have our own officers carry more of the litigation burden. May I give an example? For instance, in the year 1960, officers of the department took 90 cases in the courts,

supreme court, exchequer court, tariff board or provincial courts, which occupied 145 full days. The cost of this litigation to the government when carried out by departmental officers is, of course, less than the cost would be if we had retained outside counsel for all those cases.
Would the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I must of course emphasize that, in addition to the work they did as counsel in court, all these officers were doing other departmental work as well.

My question to the minister was simply to wonder at this point, since he has statistics about this enlargement of the role of crown employees in actual court cases, if he also had avalaible for the committee information as to the expenditure by the department for the engagement of outside counsel on a comparative basis for some years back?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe that for an answer to that question I would have to refer my hon. friend to the tabulation in the back of the estimates book under the heading "Professional and Special Services", column 4. I say this because, while all litigation on behalf of the government of Canada is conducted under instructions by the Department of Justice, the fact is that this litigation is conducted on behalf of the departments concerned and the cost of litigation is charged to the department. It is not, therefore, reflected in our estimates. The total is reflected in that item.
Would the minister give the figure for 1961-62, with his proposal in front of us for that kind of expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have just explained the reason why I am not able to give the total with respect to the Department of Justice. If, for instance, we prosecute a taxation case for the Department of National Revenue, we may well retain outside counsel but then the cost of that litigation is charged to that department. Similarly, if we prosecute a case or conduct a case on behalf of the Department of Transport, the cost of that litigation would be charged to that department. I am not able to give a precise figure. It is not reflected in the estimates of the Department of Justice.
The point I am making is that the extent to which we carry on litigation by our own officers, represents a substantial saving to the government and the people of Canada.
The hon. member for Hochelaga advanced by way of criticism the suggestion that there

is not, in the Department of Justice, a sufficiently high proportion of senior officers who are connected with the bar of the province of Quebec. This is a suggestion which I reject absolutely, and I am able to bring proof to support my statement. As I have said, there is a total of 40 legal officers in the Department of Justice. Of this total, 10 are members of the Quebec bar. In other words, one quarter of all the officers of the Department of Justice are qualified civil lawyers and members of the bar of the province of Quebec. At the deputy minister, associate or assistant deputy minister level, may I point out that we do have now a member of the bar of Quebec as associate deputy minister, one of the very senior officers of the department.
The department is now organized so that we have a deputy minister, two associate deputies and two assistant deputies. The position of associate deputy was created last year by an act approved by this house creating two such positions. We appointed to one of those positions a member of the bar of Quebec, a former director of studies in the faculty of law in the University of Ottawa. I therefore think I can say without fear of contradiction that this department recognizes full well, as indeed we should, the importance of having at our disposal and in the employ of the government of Canada a proper proportion of officers who are qualified members of the bar of Quebec with knowledge of the civil code. Indeed, we have a separate and complete section to deal with problems arising out of our field of responsibility under the civil code in the province of Quebec.
In connection with the question of whether or not there has been an unwarranted increase in senior officers, may I also point out to the committee that in 1957 and for several years prior thereto there were a deputy minister and three assistant deputy ministers, one of whom was a member of the Quebec bar. At the present time there are one deputy minister, two associate deputy ministers and two assistants. The picture is therefore not quite that which was presented by the hon. member for Hochelaga. There has not been an increase of two. There has been, in fact, an increase of only one in the senior levels of our department and I think a much more rational and logical approach to the problem of organization of the department.
Then I come to the question that was referred to by the hon. member for Hochelaga and by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, namely the matter of the control of firearms. That is an extremely difficult
Supply-Justice
question. We have had it under active study for over a year now. We have had an interdepartmental committee working on it.
Last year we referred the whole question, with certain informal suggestions arrived at by that committee, to the conference of commissioners on uniformity of legislation, criminal law section, at their meeting prior to the Canadian Bar Association meeting of last year. That conference was unable to arrive at any concrete and agreed point of view so the matter is still before us. We are examining the views of the association of police chiefs and others and it will be our intention to refer it back to the conference again this year in the hope that we may get an agreed recommendation as to what amendments should be made to the criminal law in this respect.
It will be appreciated that, although the enactment of criminal law is the responsibility of this parliament and therefore this government must take the responsibility for recommendations in that field, the enforcement is the responsibility of the provinces and views on this subject are held by large numbers of bodies including municipal as well as provincial police forces. It is therefore not a subject on which you can arrive overnight at hard and fast conclusions as to what should be done.
However, I would say this and what I have to say here is suggested by some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Hochelaga himself when he pointed out-and I am summarizing his words as I recall them-that the police in Montreal have stated that more than 2,000 persons are in illegal possession of firearms. Without for a moment denying that there may be room for improvement and appropriate amendment to the legislation, I suggest that a large part of the problem relates to enforcement. There are in existence now very definite provisions regarding the registration of firearms, making it illegal to be in possession of firearms that are not appropriately registered. Where you find, as is reported here, a responsible authority saying that more than 2,000 persons are in illegal possession of firearms, I think I am justified in saying or suggesting that the answer does not lie exclusively in another amendment to the Criminal Code. Part of the answer, at any rate, lies in the field of more vigorous enforcement of the existing provisions. Indeed, from my own thought and studies, I am led to suggest that in this matter, as in so many cases, the whole answer does not lie in enacting a criminal statute. The provinces and municipalities have authority now to license persons who may carry on certain businesses. One of the businesses that

Supply-Justice
might be subject to licence-that is the business itself-is the business of selling firearms. As I say, while not for a moment denying that there may be, and indeed there is, room for improvement in the Criminal Code of general application, I suggest that there is also very definite reason for our citizens who are concerned in this matter to ask their provincial and municipal authorities to look at their own responsibility and their own fields of jurisdiction and to ascertain whether in fact, there is not room for some improvement and control within these fields of jurisdiction.
Another matter that was of concern to several hon. members and particularly the hon. member for Hochelaga and the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont was that of goof balls. I should here emphasize the fact that this matter has been under study for some time. As far as I personally am concerned, it came forcibly to my attention first during the course of a visit to Halifax early in 1958, when, if I recall the events correctly, there had been, if not a death, then certainly some outbreak of violence, which was attributed to the sale to and the use by juveniles of goof balls. Ever since that time the matter has been increasingly of concern. I immediately raised it with my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare and again, as he has pointed out and as I have pointed out on more than one occasion, an interdepartmental committee was appointed and it has been studying the matter in the meantime. As was announced earlier by my colleague our studies are now advanced to the point where we have devised what we believe to be satisfactory legislation that will go a long way towards giving a method of control of this very dangerous situation. That legislation will be introduced into this house by my colleague, as I understand it, within a matter of the next few days or probably at the latest within another week. I hope the house will find that it represents a great forward step in the control of the problem of goof balls.
I recognize the fact that it is a matter of years since the problem first began to be discussed and first began to be one of real concern to municipal and other responsible agencies. I can only say that in fields such as this effective and acceptable legislation is not a matter of hasty drafting or hasty enactment. Here you are dealing with a problem of drugs, namely barbiturates which, legally and properly used are perfectly proper and legal and indeed salutary medicinal aids. You therefore do not enact out of hand and without consideration legislation which will make their use illegal or ban them in certain circumstances and in certain cases. Legislation IMr. Fulton.]
of this type requires exhaustive and careful study and consultation between representatives of the department of health and welfare, the medical profession, the police and other enforcement agencies, municipal bodies, licensing bodies and so on before you can come up with a statute which you can with confidence recommend to the House of Commons as being appropriate legislation to enact. So I have no apologies to make for the time it has taken. I believe we now have satisfactory legislation which will be introduced in a matter of a few days by my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
On the question of rehabilitation, which was also referred to by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, I have only this to say. I am in thorough agreement with what he himself said on that score. Indeed our whole penal reform program, designed as it is to enable us to rehabilitate so far as we can the inmates of our institutions, is of greatly diminished value if, having done that, we find that those who leave our institutions as, we hope, better men than when they went in, are not accepted in society. That will undo and negate the whole purpose of the program and I have been at pains in all my public speeches on this matter, wherever appropriate, to emphasize the responsibility of society in this regard as well as the responsibility of government.
The responsibility of government is a responsibility on behalf of society to design and implement effective programs of training and rehabilitation, but we cannot fulfil the role of society itself, which is the role of understanding and of acceptance. What we can do is ensure so far as possible that when a man comes out he is ready to resume his place in society; but unless society is prepared to give him a chance, the best program in the world will be defeated.
All I can say there is that I agree thoroughly with what the hon. member has said and express the hope that as our correctional reform program becomes better understood, and as its results become more obvious, there will be a corresponding and increasing acceptance by society of those who are what I might call the graduates of that program. But with respect to the program itself, as I have said, I would prefer to wait until we reach the penitentiary item, when I shall be able to make what I think will be an interesting and encouraging report to the committee on the progress made to date.

Mr. Chairman, there are a number of questions I should like to put to the minister, in general covering the area of his responsibility. I should like to start off by asking him what his view of this particular statement is:

"Too often and for too long in this country one of the qualifications of a judge, aside from ability, is political competence... I suggest that a move towards elevating the judiciary would be a declaration by the attorney general and Minister of Justice of the country that from now on, within reasonable limitations, political qualifications shall take second place to ability, capacity, judgment and the possession of the faculties that result in a judiciary so necessary to the maintenance of our security and our freedom".
I suppose the minister recognizes that statement and knows who made it. It was made by the present Prime Minister, in 1948, and it is contained in an editorial in the Gazette of February 7, 1961. I want to ask the minister, in relation to the vacancies and the opportunities which exist, whether he agrees with this point of view expressed by the Prime Minister and whether he can assure us that at least a portion of the judiciary he has appointed or is planning to appoint is not composed primarily of members of the Conservative party.
We would be very interested in knowing, in view of this high-minded statement made by the Prime Minister, whether the minister can indicate if some of them are absolutely not connected in any way with politics. I ask this question just as a matter of interest.
I wish to ask another question in this same field but perhaps from a different point of view. The other day the Associate Minister of National Defence was very candid to us in the house in pointing out that, like the Liberal opposition when they were in power, this government recognized its friends; it could see its friends more quickly than it could its opponents.
In relation to the lawyers that the minister hires, I wonder whether he could give us the assurance that those lawyers who are being hired and who have been hired to handle these various cases of which he gave us statistics are friends of the government in the sense that-well, I think the minister understands the sense in which I speak. I ask this question because so often people say to me, "Why is it that there seem to be so many lawyers in politics?"; meaning, I suppose, not necessarily as active politicians but associated with parties. In all the small towns and smaller cities they seem to form the nucleus of the structure of either the Liberal or the Conservative party. The other day when I was in Peterborough somebody was setting out who the bigshots were in the Liberal and Conservative parties. In each case it seemed to be a little cluster of lawyers.
What is wrong with Frank Scott?

Someone says, "What is wrong with that?" I am not suggesting there is anything wrong with that, but I am always
Supply-J ustice
looking for an explanation to give people who raise these questions. One of the answers I always give is, "Look", as Marx said, "for the cash nexus". It pays a lawyer to be connected with one of the "in" parties, and especially one that is going to be in because he can count on getting some work from them. I just wondered whether the minister could assure us that these fees which are paid to outside lawyers are not only going to lawyers throughout Canada who are friends of the party.
The other question I wanted to ask the minister was this. I wondered whether the minister could give us some report of his negotiations with the attorneys general of the provinces in relation to ways to amend the British North America Act. It is very difficult to understand what is happening by following the press reports, and I do not believe the minister has given the house a comprehensive statement in this regard. It is very difficult for us to appreciate just what are the obstacles and what are the positions of the various parties. I know the minister would not want to interpret what may be the position of Saskatchewan, Quebec or Ontario, but perhaps he could give us some idea of the negotiations which have taken place and what the difficulties seem to be that are preventing a breakthrough.
There is one other point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister, and I must in a sense apologize to him for this. Several years ago when the minister introduced amendments to the Criminal Code relating to obscene publications I was one of those who feared that this could open the door to a great deal of censorship of material that had literary merit. However, so far the legislation has been almost completely ineffective, and I say quite candidly that I am delighted that this is so.
One of the things I have come to appreciate more and more is that if censorship in Canada is to get any real toe-hold it will be done through the Department of National Revenue and the customs officials. I am delighted to see that in this particular area the present minister has been much more liberal than ministers and officials of the previous government. I am not saying this lightly or without any-

Mr. Chairman, I wonder what the hon. member means by saying that the legislation has not been effective. Presumably this legislation was designed to keep out smut and salacious literature. If this material is not coming in, the legislation is being effective.

My point with regard to this, as the hon. member knows from what I said last year when the legislation was going

Supply-Justice
through, is that these amendments to the Criminal Code could put into the hands of very narrow minded justices, and particularly magistrates, in provincial jurisdictions powers that would ultimately lead to the censoring of material for the whole country.
I am very pleased to see that, so far as I have been able to find out, there has only been one case. That is in a sense one where there is a really ridiculous element, because I have learned from the publishers that there are at least 250,000 copies of this particular book, D. H. Lawrence's "Lady Chat-terley's Lover", in Canada at the present time. I have an estimate by several publishers that there are at least 250,000 copies of that book in Canada. That is a tremendous circulation for any book to achieve at the present time in this country, so it would be really ironical if any judicial process were to lead to the banning of a book so many copies of which are already in existence here.
One of the aspects of smut or pornography with which the legislation was supposed to deal used to obsess the minister a good deal when he was sitting in this house as a private member; I refer to the field of comics, and picture magazines dealing with various sadistic poses and various aspects usually of the female form. I, myself, could wish that the legislation had been more effective in dealing with publications of this type. I know that in Ontario the attorney general has set up a most curious quartet of people whose job it is to advise him as to what is on the newsstands and to examine any material which they believe should be brought to the attention of the attorney general as likely to provide grounds for proceeding, as I understand it, under this part of the Criminal Code. Again according to my understanding of how this arrangement is working out, in over two years this quartet has still not made a single recommendation. I am not being critical of this but I do know they have had huge quantities of these picture magazines before them-all the various things that are put forward as obscene and pornographic-but as yet they have come to no decisions. Some of my more literary friends may say: that is excellent; we are not having any control or censorship, and you should be grateful. But I should like to make a distinction between work with literary or artistic merit, put together within some kind of covers, behind which stand the names of an author and a publisher and the kind of material, particularly of a sadistic nature, which appears in so many of those so-called men's magazines.
I am certainly not suggesting that we do not need this particular amendment any

longer, but I should like to hear from the minister some comment concerning the operation of this section of the Criminal Code and perhaps some explanation from him as to why it has been generally ineffective. It may seem paradoxical that I should welcome the effectiveness of the section as far as books are concerned while being a little disturbed by its lack of effectiveness in the field or men's magazines or the sadistic kind of monthly pot boilers.
Another point I should like to make underlines the reason why in my opinion the minister should give the committee an explanation. If he would recall what he said when he introduced this change in the Criminal Code, I think he will remember using the argument that one reason for this change was that it would lead to the removal of pulp trash from the newsstands. That was the main objective, as I recall it, of the change which was made at that time. I think that is a fair paraphrase of the position he took; the account which appeared in the Globe and Mail, at least, confirms my recollection. For this reason I should like to know how this legislation is working out in practice. I realize that the minister could say that this, after all, is something which must be worked out under provincial jurisdiction by the provincial authorities themselves, but it seems to me that to take such an attitude would not be good enough in the light of the promises the minister made at the time the change was introduced. He cannot now wash his hands of what was done. Perhaps he will be able to correct my impression that the amendment is not working very well, but in any case I think he owes the committee an explanation of what is happening.
There are some further remarks I should like to make in relation to the R.C.M.P. and to the Combines Investigation Act but I will wait until the appropriate point is reached in our study of the estimates. I must say, however, that I was startled by the minister's remarks reported from Toronto the other day to the effect-if I may paraphrase them- "please, Mr. Fulton, keep a file on me and some day I shall be able to show how innocent I am". There is an irony in this which I hope the minister will explain when we come to the estimates of the R.C.M.P. I should also like to ask the minister if he would consider giving an explanation which he has come close to making a couple of times in past years about not what is in the file but how the files are retired in so far as the security investigation branch is concerned. It seems to me the minister indicated three or four sessions ago that work was going along to develop a new standard of

appraisal of the files which are kept. I should like to hear later from the hon. gentleman what he has to say on this subject.

Mr. Chairman, I wish at the beginning of my remarks to congratulate the Minister of Justice on the recent announcements which he has made regarding the adoption of a new attitude towards the rehabilitation of criminals. This enlightened attitude towards inmates serving their sentence in penal institutions deserves great praise because rehabilitation is emphasized and the positive aspect of penal servitude is stressed. I can appreciate the research which is being done by the Department of Justice into all phases of crime and delinquency and I commend the minister for the vigorous leadership which he has given in instituting these long needed studies and reforms. Notwithstanding the great amount of research which has been done into the problems of crime and delinquency, I feel that there is one area in which we still have insufficient information and that is in the field of drug addiction.
The minister will remember that last year, during the discussions of his estimates, I took the opportunity to put on record my grave concern about this problem. I pointed out that out of some 3,400 drug addicts in Canada, half are found in British Columbia and more particularly in the city of Vancouver, and most of their activities appear to revolve around a certain area in my riding of Vancouver Centre.
I mentioned then that there appeared to be a growing number of juvenile addicts. In 1957 for example, there were 25 teenagers in Canada who were drug addicts. In 1958, there were 47, and in 1959 the number had increased to 55. British Columbia had the dubious distinction of having the majority of those teen-age addicts because of the figure of 55, 46 are to be found in my province. I also said and I quote:
It would appear therefore that apart from teenager addicts there is some tendency towards stabilization in the number of addicts.
I expressed concern for the growing number of teen-age addicts last year and I am afraid that my fears have been justified because in the fifth annual report covering 1960-61 of the narcotic addiction foundation of British Columbia in Vancouver, British Columbia, the report of the director to the chairman of the board of directors disclosed that the number of young people voluntarily seeking help from the foundation had increased from the previous year. This is what the director's report had to say, and I quote:
The age groups of under 20, and 20-25 years showed an increased percentage of the total, and would tend to confirm the impression that the
Supply-Justice
age of onset of addiction is being reduced, i.e., younger people are being more exposed to addicting drugs than they were say five to ten years ago.
A questionnaire compiled by the foundation which was completed by 330 young people in Vancouver revealed information which is disquieting in its implications. For example, 19.5 per cent of the 18 year old males admitted having had the opportunity of using heroin. Of all the persons questioned, 56 per cent stated that they had had their opportunity to use heroin when they were drinking.
The questionnaire created some controversy in Vancouver, and some quarters have questioned the interpretation of the results of that questionnaire. Without entering into the merits of the argument, I feel that the foundation should be congratulated for having the courage to persist in conducting research into this most complicated problem.
The 330 young people who received the questionnaire included persons in the 15 to 18 year old group. Some of the information gained is startling. For example, 12.9 per cent of the 17 year old girls believe that there is no harm in occasionally using heroin, and to the question "Have you had an opportunity to use heroin yourself?", 5.9 per cent of the females aged 16, 11.6 per cent of males aged 17, and 19.5 per cent of males aged 18 replied "Yes".
Another question was included dealing with the availability of illegal drugs. It asked "Do you think you could get some narcotic drug illegally if you wanted to?" To this question 47.9 per cent of 16 year old males, 38.9 per cent of 17 year old females and 66.6 per cent of 18 year old males replied "Yes". These figures are alarming, and I hope there will be an opportunity to conduct a more comprehensive program of education and research.
The Vancouver Sun on May 3, 1961 reported that the senior councillor of the foundation stated that of the 285 addicts treated at the foundation during a two year period, it was disclosed that almost one half the group were addicted before their twentieth birthday, and he estimates that there are now 200 addicts under the age of 21 in Vancouver. I shall have more to say on this subject when the narcotics bill is brought forward by the minister.
I should now like to say a few words regarding the subject of increasing the salaries of judges. Let me say at the outset that, while I believe the salaries of judges are, by and large, already adequate, bearing in mind the generous pension provisions, I feel there is one class of judge which deserves an increase. I refer to county court judges.
I am well aware that the work of the county court judges varies across the country,

Supply-J ustice
so I base my remarks in regard to the work done by those county court judges serving in Vancouver. I do not want it thought that I feel that the judges of the supreme courts of the provinces, or of the courts of appeal, are not deserving of salary increases, but at this time I think a more urgent case can be made in respect of county court judges. County court judges now receive salaries of $10,500 per year. The jurisdiction of these county court judges is very extensive, and compared with the salaries paid to others, I suggest there is some justification for an increase.
For example, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration has set up a series of naturalization courts across Canada. The presiding judges receive $11,000 per year. As well as the presiding judge, there is an administrator, a principal clerk, senior clerk, a clerk and a stenographer collecting sala-aries totalling $24,000. Prior to the establishment of these naturalization courts applications for naturalization were heard by county court judges who performed this duty along with their other duties at the salary of $10,500 per year. These judges were assisted by a grade III clerk and a grade I stenographer in the court registry, these two persons receiving salaries totalling $6,000 per year.
I am not casting any aspersions on the judges of the naturalization courts, but it does seem unfair to me that for performing one duty they receive more than a county court judge who has a very wide jurisdiction and, under the Criminal Code and provincial summary conviction act sits as a court of appeal where, by way of re-hearing, hears appeals from judgments of police and stipendiary magistrates. The responsibility of the county court judge is very heavy in these cases, because his decision on the facts is final.
The city of Vancouver has six magistrates with salaries, according to seniority, ranging as follows: $15,000, $13,500, $12,500, and two at $10,750. Some of the junior city prosecutors are in receipt of salaries exceeding those of county court judges. With comparisons such as those, I believe a good case can be made for increasing the salary of county court judges, and I sincerely hope the minister will give sympathetic consideration to my request on behalf of this group of citizens who are forbidden to speak for themselves but who, none the less, have answered a call of duty no less than have members of parliament.
Finally, I should like to say something about the R.C.M.P. investigation into the illegal entry of some Chinese into Canada. In so doing, I want to urge those Chinese, who have entered the country illegally, to come forward and regularize their status.

Hon. members will recall that, almost one year ago, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration made a statement in the house to the effect that it was not the intention of this government, in connection with the current investigation, to prosecute or deport from the country any Chinese presently in Canada who have not themselves engaged in assisting other Chinese, apart from their own relatives, to enter Canada illegally. It is reasonable to assume that the R.C.M.P. must have had knowledge of these irregular entries. It is also reasonable to assume that if the R.C.M.P. were to proceed against these people in the usual manner, a substantial number of arrests would be made.
There are some individuals who think, because the R.C.M.P. have not made mass arrests, the government does not have any real evidence of large scale illegal immigration. Others construe the lack of arrests as a sign of weakness on the part of the government. Arguments have also been advanced that these Chinese people really have not broken the law in telling minor lies. I should be the first to agree that it would be very difficult to make out a moral case against the majority of these Chinese, because the Immigration Act, as it stands, was, and is, unduly restrictive.
I suggest that if the Immigration Act had permitted the early Chinese immigrants to bring their wives into Canada with them, none of this trouble would have started. Anyone who has been away from home for a long time, as for example, during the war, can understand how lonely persons can become after a few months' separation from their families. Imagine the unhappy state of affairs for those Chinese who were separated often as long as 20, 30 or 40 years from their wives and families. I suggest that had wives been allowed to come in, any children born would have been properly registered under Canadian law, and there should not have been the opportunity to create a fictitious family, which has made it possible for illegal immigration.
In so far as the actions of those people, who were prompted by a desire to rejoin their familities, are concerned, it is very difficult to make out any kind of a moral case against them, particularly when they have been good and law abiding citizens since their arrival. I want to emphasize the fact that I limit my remarks to those individuals whose illegal actions were prompted by a desire to rejoin their families, because there is a suggestion that in some cases being re-united with the family was not the guiding motive.

In an article dated April 29, 1961, written by Mr. Robert McKeown, an eminent writer, entitled "How Chinese Are Smuggled Into Canada" he states:
But the facts that have come to light through the current investigation seem to indicate that in relatively few cases is strong family feeling the basis for illegal immigration. The real cause of the racket is the money to be made from it.
It may be that such is the case, Mr. Chairman, but in all the cases that I have brought to the attention of the department a family relationship was established. I am not denying the truth of Mr. McKeown's statement, but because of my experience in a substantial number of these cases I want to put on record my impression that reunification with the family or some member of the family was the underlying factor. Indeed, in an article also published on April 29, 1961, in the same Weekend Magazine and entitled, "I Was An Illegal Immigrant", the author of that story said that his father died in the war with Japan and that his grandfather who had been in Canada since 1910 had helped his mother and brother by sending money and it was his grandfather who conceived the idea of him coming to Canada. Why did this young man come to Canada? Because his grandfather obviously could not go on forever supporting him, his brother and mother. As this anonymous author said, "I am working again in a restaurant and sending money to help my family who have got to Hong Kong from Toy Shan. My grandfather helped them for so long and it is right that I should help them now."
I think the government recognizes that there is this difficult humanitarian problem and that is why the minister announced the amnesty provision. It is not and has not been the intention of the government to prosecute those who came into the country illegally if that person was not an active agent engaged in making financial gain from such transactions. I can speak from personal knowledge in this regard because not one of those people whom I have advised to make voluntary statements has been arrested, fined, or deported by the Canadian authorities.
By regularizing their status these people can resume their proper names and identities and they can be granted proper landed status. In time they will also be able to apply for the admission into Canada of members of their family. The heavy fear of arrest is also removed and they are able to enjoy the benefits of living in this country. However, there has been some reluctance on the part of some to come forward because they fear that they will implicate others whom they consider as friends and benefactors.
Supply-Justice
Those who come forward voluntarily and make a full statement have everything to gain. This government, far from prosecuting the Chinese in Canada, has taken the unprecedented step of extending amnesty. But the period of amnesty cannot, in my opinion, go on forever. No matter how charitable a government may be, you cannot hope forever for special treatment when, after all, the law has been broken. Unfair though these immigration laws may have been and no matter how strong a moral case may be advanced for the actions of certain Chinese, the fact remains that the law has been broken. Two wrongs do not make a right.
It may well be that if more people in the Chinese communities across Canada had worked together earlier in order to urge a change in the immigration laws, these unfortunate incidents might not have happened. One could be tempted to say that such representations were made by certain individuals but they were not well received by the previous administration. If I were to say that, I would also point out that we in this party have not done as much for Chinese immigration as I had hoped, even though I understand that the present act is being amended.
The R.C.M.P. have had a difficult task in this investigation. By and large I think their conduct is commendable. However, I have reports that some who have worked with them in this investigation have not fully understood their position, but it is my understanding that where such cases have been reported prompt action has been taken to ensure that those persons concerned were instructed as to the exact nature of their duties and their spheres of responsibility.
I think that the R.C.M.P. have acted with great restraint because under section 16 of the Immigration Act they can arrest anyone whom they have reason to suspect of being in the country illegally. The power is there. The fact that the R.C.M.P. have not used it should not be construed as lack of evidence. Far from showing weakness, I think that the government is demonstrating a high degree of sympathy and I would be reluctant to think that advantage was being taken of this attitude and that the investigations were being unduly delayed by passive non-co-operation.
I regret that I have spoken at length on this subject. You can appreciate, Mr. Chairman, that it is a painful subject for me. But because I believe strongly that the law must be obeyed no matter how unpleasant it may be or until such time as it is changed, and also because I feel that Chinese who have entered the country illegally have nothing to lose and everything to gain by regularizing their status, I have taken this opportunity

Supply-Justice
to bring these facts before the house so that we will all exercise moderation and understanding in this difficult time in the history of the Chinese communities in Canada.

May I ask the hon. member a question? I appreciated his statement, but he indicated that there might be in the future, and he did not define what he meant by the future, a time when this immunity might cease. He has closer connections with the Minister of Justice than I have these days and I wonder whether he would indicate to the committee what his opinion is as to the possible time when this immunity might cease?

Surely the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River would not expect me to announce government policy. I think that question should properly be directed to the minister. What I have said is based purely on my own personal assessment of the situation as I see it.

Mr. Chairman, I want to take a few minutes to reply to one of the arguments the minister made this afternoon. Before the committee rose for the supper recess the minister ridiculed Bill No. C-76 which I introduced on March 22. He said the bill was a monstrosity, that it did not accomplish anything, that it merely repealed an act and re-enacted it again and therefore it was a farce. The minister makes bald announcements but he never backs them up with any quotations or evidence and he never cites any authorities to support his words. The minister's pronouncements do not become truth just because the minister utters them. I am not prepared to accord infallibility to the minister and the more I listen to him the more convinced I am of his fallibility.
I should like to put before the committee this evening two precedents that I think are analogous to the bill which the minister has described as a farce and a monstrosity. There was a time before the Statute of Westminster was enacted when certain laws of the British parliament applied in Canada. The Canadian government did not like that situation and sought to remedy it. So certain laws were passed which we thought would correct the situation. In one instance we brought into effect a section of the Criminal Code, the old section 1025, I believe, which contained a clause that there would be no appeal from any sentence or judgment passed under that section.
Another one was the Supreme Court Act which contained a clause to the effect that the judgment of the supreme court would be final. In spite of all this, these laws were not effective in supplying remedies because

they were declared ultra vires. In spite of our own laws which we had passed here in parliament, cases and appeals were still taken to the British privy council.
Finally, the Statute of Westminster was passed-I think it was about 1931-and that statute contained a clause giving effect to future laws passed in this House of Commons from that time forward. But the Statute of Westminster validated only future laws that were passed in this house. It had an effect on future laws similar to the effect the bill of rights will have on laws passed in the future after the bill of rights was put on the statute books. There is quite a good analogy there.
These two examples which I have cited, the section of the Criminal Code and the appropriate clause of the Supreme Court Act, were brought before this house, repealed and re-enacted in exactly the same way as I sought to do through Bill No. C-76. If what I sought to do was a monstrosity and a farce, well, there is a very good precedent for it. It was necessary to follow this course because the Statute of Westminster applied only to future laws, so the old law had to be re-enacted. It was re-enacted in exactly the same form. There may have been a change in a word or a phrase, but there was no change in the intent, no change in the meaning and no change in the force of the old act. To all intents and purposes, it was exactly the same old bill which was brought in, repealed and re-enacted. This is what the minister says is a farce and a monstrosity.
Just as the Statute of Westminster was not in existence when the old laws were passed and future laws came under its influence, so there was no bill of rights in effect when the old Fisheries Act was passed but the passage of the bill of rights created a new situation which was similar to the situation created by the passage of the Statute of Westminster. I cite these cases to the minister, and I ask him to place on Hansard similar authorities, similar precedents, to bolster the argument he has made.
The minister keeps shifting his ground. He does not reply to the arguments that are made. The other day when the minister intervened in the debate with relation to the amendment to the Fisheries Act, he said Bill No. C-76 was not properly before the house. Today when the hon. member for Skeena had him backed into a corner by intimating the minister had been derelict in his duty by not submitting a report on the bill as the law required, he shifted his ground and said a decision had not been made. There was no ruling as to whether or not Bill No. C-76 was

properly before the house. This question was still under consideration by Mr. Speaker and by the house leader. Well, this bill was introduced on March 22 and today is May 25, which means this consideration has been going on for eight weeks.
I am, therefore, a bit curious about this report the minister is required to make under the bill of rights examination regulations and when the minister replies I want to inform the committee just exactly what the purpose of this report is. If the committee is not to make use of it or if we are not to have the benefit of it in considering legislation that comes before the house, what purpose does the report serve? I want to tell the committee that when I introduced the bill I did so in good faith. When the minister replied to my argument this afternoon, he kept emphasizing only one part of my statement. I said that I had introduced this bill to bring it into conformity with the bill of rights but I also stated it was to bring it into conformity with the report which the minister was obliged to make on this bill.
I could have followed my own ideas about changes in the bill which I thought might take care of any inconsistencies with the bill of rights. However, if there is to be a report handed down by experts who have studied not only the particular clauses in which I was interested but the whole bill, surely the sensible thing to do if we want to do a good job on this legislation as we put it through the house, is to get the best ideas we can about it. If I made a mistake, it was in taking the minister's report at face value. I thought it meant something and I thought it was for the purpose of guiding the members of the house in doing the best job we could on the legistlation that comes before us. If that is not the purpose of the report, I cannot see what other useful purpose it serves. I certainly would like to have the minister enlighten me on this point when he replies.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity to call the minister's attention to the rather irregular way the R.C.M.P. carries out certain investigations.
I have been told that, with the help of the food and drug branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare, the R.C.M.P. makes investigations in establishments where pharmaceutical products are sold, especially in retail drug stores. Yet, the way the constables do their work, they should not be called investigators but instigators. Indeed, under false pretences, they succeed in getting special drugs from people who act in good
Supply-Justice
faith, professional pharmacists whose only care is to exercise their profession conscientiously and do their duty by serving the public well.
Constables present themselves as sick people and pretend they have forgotten their medical prescription or that they are strangers visiting relatives and that they urgently need the drugs. They play on the druggist's sympathies so that the latter, moved by their plight agrees to give them without a prescription, drugs which call for one.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw the minister's attention to two particular cases which happened recently in the Sherbrooke district, in the province of Quebec. R.C.M.P. constables went to a drugstore and told the pharmacist that they were on a trip and did not have a medical prescription for certain drugs they wanted. Out of sympathy for those supposedly sick people, the druggist gave them 12 tablets. Needless to say, that in both cases, the R.C.M.P. laid charges against the pharmacists who are highly respected in the profession and who render great services to the public. They were brought before the court and had to pay a nominal fine but it remains, sir, that this use of false pretence with druggists who act in good faith, who are conscious of their obligations, is what I would call a disgusting behaviour, if it did not reflect upon those who use such means to succeed in their investigations.
Consequently, I would ask the Minister of Justice if he could not impress upon the R.C.M.P. that its constables who are in the employ of the Department of Justice should not instigate honest people to break the law.
